title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
We all know that LLMs tend to make errors, whether it be simple mistakes (e.g., improper arithmetic), hallucinations, or something else. But, studying the statistics of mistakes that LLMs make shows us something that we might not intuitively expect.
Background: One way to study the mistakes made by LLMs is to leverage prompt ensembles. Put simply, these are sets of diverse prompts that are meant to solve the same problem. If we ask the LLM to solve a problem using several different prompts within an ensemble, we can study the LLM’s behavior, as well as measure mistakes that are made across different prompts. This was done in the “Ask Me Anything” (AMA) paper, which explores the use of prompt ensembles to improve LLM reliability in solving complex (reasoning-based) problems.
Prompt Sensitivity: The analysis by AMA shows us that the LLM’s accuracy will fluctuate based on the prompt we use. Within a prompt ensemble, we see a ~10% average variation in accuracy across different prompts. Given that all prompts within an ensemble are meant to solve a similar problem, this shows us that LLM performance is a sensitive to the exact wording used in a prompt! We need to craft/curate the “perfect prompt” to get the best performance.
What types of errors do LLMs make? However, we find out something even more interesting if we study the Jaccard index of errors made by LLMs over a prompt ensemble. Consider the following quote:
“Using [prompt ensembles], we see 9.5% average variation in accuracy and that the Jaccard index over errors is 69% higher than if prompt errors were i.i.d.” - from AMA paper
To rephrase the above statement, the errors that LLMs make are not randomly distributed! Rather, LLM errors tend to cluster around a single, incorrect response. This is a huge problem for strategies like self-consistency that use majority votes over multiple LLM generations to derive a final answer.
TL;DR: When LLMs make mistakes, they are not random. Interestingly, the mistakes made by LLMs tend to cluster around a single wrong answer, which can be quite counterintuitive and misleading. Thus, it’s important to have this in mind when building with LLMs and leveraging reliability techniques like prompt ensembles and self-consistency.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The Falcon-7B/40B open-source LLMs were released late this week, and their performance is super impressive. But, there's a huge catch for those using them commercially! Here's my main takeaways from the models so far...
model architecture. The Falcon models were released by UAE's technology innovation institute. Falcon includes two models: a 40 billion parameter variant and a smaller, 7 billion parameter model. The architecture of Falcon uses both flash attention and multi-query attention (see thread for paper links). Put simply, this means the architecture can perform inference super quickly---5X more efficient than GPT-3 at inference time!
data quality. Authors of Falcon put a heavy emphasis on training the model over high-quality data.
"A particular focus was put on data quality at scale. LLMs are notoriously sensitive to the quality of their training data, so significant care was taken in building a data pipeline that would both scale to tens of thousands of CPU cores for fast processing, and that would extract high-quality content from the web using extensive filtering and deduplication."
By combining this high-quality data pipeline with improvements in architectural efficiency, Falcon LLMs are trained using only 75% of GPT-3's compute budget despite performing much better.
performance. Beyond its efficiency, Falcon performs super well. It currently beats all other open-source models on LLM leaderboards! Notably, the performance of Falcon-40B surpasses that of popular open-source models like LLaMA, MPT, and RedPajama. The combination of inference efficiency and impressive performance makes the Falcon models pretty impressive and useful. Instruction-tuned versions of Falcon (e.g., Falcon-40B-Instruct) have also been recently released.
the catch. Falcon seems great, but there's a huge catch if you want to use it commercially. These models were released on a modified Apache 2.0 license called the TII Falcon LLM License. Notably, this license requires that all derivatives of the model (e.g., includes the model, any fine-tuned versions of it, etc.) that are used in commercial applications must pay royalties for such use. This is a new and interesting agreement for open-source LLMs that we have not seen before!
"Note that this license contains obligations on those of you who are commercially exploiting Falcon LLM or any Derivative Work to make royalty payments."
TL;DR: Falcon LLMs are awesome and a huge step forward for the open-source LLM movement. However, I'm not personally convinced that this royalty payment model will be viable. In my opinion, the open-source community is incredibly likely to just continue releasing high-quality models that are completely open-source. Personally, I would not yet consider using Falcon over impressive models like MPT-7B (at least in anything with commercial applications). The difference in performance would have to be massive for me to pay royalties for the use of any LLM. If I'm going to be paying, why not just use GPT-4?

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Language models can solve a variety of complex tasks accurately, but they struggle with certain functionality that we, as humans, consider basic. Are LLMs doomed to suffer these limitations forever? The short answer is no! We can improve these models by giving them access to external tools.
Quick Analogy: Many advancements in the human race have been catalyzed by access to new and innovative tools (e.g., the printing press or computer). Similar to how humans become better with access to tools, LLMs become more capable when given access to a set of simple APIs that can provide useful information or perform tasks for them. Why would we rely 100% on an LLM to solve everything, when we can delegate difficult tasks to a more accurate and specialized tool? We can use such an approach to mitigate problems that are constantly encountered with these models, such as incorrect information within the output or a lack of temporal reasoning skills.
What kind of tools are useful? To understand what kinds of tools are useful for LLMs, we can consider some of their major limitations:
- Lack of access to up-to-date information
- Tendency to hallucinate (i.e., output incorrect information)
- Difficulties with evaluating mathematical expressions
- Incomplete understanding of low-resource languages
- Inability to understand the progression of time
When struggling to solve a problem, it is often useful for an LLM to query an external tool that can provide more context. Tools are incredibly useful whenever providing extra information or context can help an LLM with solving a problem. Examples of useful tools include information retrieval system, code interpreters, calendar apps, calculators, or even translation modules.
Teaching LLMs to use tools: One method of teaching an LLM to use tools was proposed by the Toolformer paper. Interestingly, we see that the LLM can learn to leverage these tools in a completely end-to-end manner. The model decides what APIs to call, which arguments to pass to these APIs, and how to best use the information that is returned without any hard-coded control flows. To do this, we curate a dataset of training data that demonstrates the proper use of these tools. In the Toolformer paper, this dataset is created automatically using a self-supervised heuristic—meaning that no human intervention is required—that requires only a few examples of usage for each tool. Then, we fine-tune the LLM over this data, allowing it to learn the correct usage of each tool.
TL;DR: Connecting LLMs to external tools is a really popular topic right now, and this technique works well for solving common limitations with LLMs! The Toolformer paper shows us that we can easily teach LLMs how to use tools via a fine-tuning approach. Plus, we can construct a fine-tuning dataset for tool following by bootstrapping/prompting existing LLMs, which minimizes human annotation effort!

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
As researchers learn more about LLMs, the (rough) analogies that can be made to humans become quite interesting. One topic that has really fascinated me is using groups of LLMs (or multiple outputs from a single LLM) to arrive at a more accurate answer, as compared to generating a single output from an LLM.
Some background: One notable reliability technique that can be used for LLMs is called self-consistency. Put simply, this technique uses a single LLM to generate multiple answers for a question. Then, we arrive at a final answer by taking a majority vote over several outputs from the LLM.
LLMs cluster around bad answers: This technique works well, but it has an interesting property: the LLM does not make mistakes randomly. Rather, we usually see that the LLM, if it is incorrect, will output the same incorrect answer multiple times when using a self-consistency approach. This is a problem because the majority vote in this case is wrong. The LLMs output clusters around a unified, incorrect answer.
A practical example: A recent research paper put this to the test by asking GPT-4 questions about a specialized domain: radiation oncology. The model was provided five different instructions (i.e., an ensemble of different prompts to solve the same question) to solve each question, then a majority vote was taken over the response to each prompt. However, using such a prompt ensemble barely improved performance, indicating that the LLM is indeed clustering around incorrect answers.
What about for humans? When we think about analogies to humans, we might initially think that a similar finding would apply to large groups of humans. One example of this is the groupthink bias. When a bunch of people get together to make a decision, they can end up clustering around a bad decision proposed by others for the sole purpose of achieving harmony. Personal opinions are set aside to adopt the opinion of the group.
The reality: Interestingly, however, humans experience a completely opposite effect! When a team of medical physicists (i.e., experts in this area) combine together to form a majority vote for each question, the performance is much better than each expert answering questions in isolation.
“Although ChatGPT (GPT-4) performed well overall, its intrinsic properties did not allow for further improvement when scoring based on a majority vote across trials. In contrast, a team of medical physicists were able to greatly outperform ChatGPT (GPT-4) using a majority vote.” - from
The takeaway: Generic LLMs do not seem to benefit from a majority vote strategy when answering questions in specialized domains (or even on generic reasoning benchmarks). On the other hand, expert humans do experience a massive benefit from this strategy. This yields the question: will specialized LLMs benefit more from ensembling strategies? The answer is unclear (for now) but quite interesting to consider. In my opinion, it seems totally possible that specialized LLMs (i.e., domain experts) may benefit more than generic LLMs from such a technique.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Foundation models are a popular topic in AI research. However, task-specific fine-tuning outperforms zero/few-shot learning with foundation models in most cases. Specialized models are hard to beat! Luckily, recent research indicates that we can combine the strengths of both approaches...
LLMs + Tools: Combining language models with external tools (e.g., calculators, search engines, retrieval mechanisms, etc.) is a popular and effective approach for making these models more capable and effective. This approach is being explored via research advances like the Toolformer and even by OpenAI with the ChatGPT plugins store. Interestingly, integrating language models with useful tools is becoming quite simple. We can do it entirely via a prompting approach that provides descriptions of available tools and relies upon in-context learning capabilities to deduce the proper usage of each tool.
Deep Learning as a Tool: For a while, research on language models only considered integration with relatively simple tools. What if we instead considered integrating language models with other, specialized deep learning models? The AI/ML community places a heavy emphasis on open-source software, meaning that many of the most powerful deep learning models are freely available online. Usually, these models come with well-written descriptions, called model cards, that can be used to provide all needed information about any model to an LLM. Then, these models can be easily integrated with an LLM via basic prompting techniques.
How can we do this? Deep learning models that are available on platforms like HuggingFace can be accessed via their associated model APIs. By teaching language models to call APIs associated with other, specialized deep learning models, we can construct a system that uses the language model as a controller (or brain) to coordinate the solution of a problem by planning and delegating subtasks to different APIs.
“By providing only the model descriptions, HuggingGPT can continuously and conveniently integrate diverse expert models from AI communities, without altering any structure or prompt settings. This open and continuous manner brings us one step closer to realizing artificial general intelligence.” - from HuggingGPT
Some Examples: Two recent publications have attempted to realize the goal of integrating language models with other deep learning models. HuggingGPT leverages paid APIs (e.g., for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) and a prompting approach to teach language models to leverage specialized models available via HuggingFace. This approach works well, but it is highly dependent upon the capabilities of the underlying language model and only works for a fixed number of well-documented model APIs. Gorilla explores a more reliable and large-scale approach via open-source models (i.e., LLaMA-7B) and fine-tuning. More specifically, it curates a fine-tuning dataset of over 1,600 different model APIs, then fine-tunes an open-source language model (using the self-instruct framework) to learn how to leverage these APIs. The resulting Gorilla model is surprisingly capable of leveraging many different model APIs to solve complex problems. Plus, it can even adapt to real-time changes in model documentation by leveraging a retrieval-aware fine-tuning approach.
TL;DR: There are a lot of “narrow expert” deep learning models out there that solve tasks extremely accurately. Modern large language models take an orthogonal approach of solving many different problems with a single model—they are foundation models! Both of these approaches are viable, and we can combine them by using language models as a controller that learns to call the APIs of specialized models when solving a problem.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Language models are known to struggle with solving certain types of problems, but it seems like many of these limitations are being solved as more powerful models are created and released. Various prompting practices and popular techniques are quickly becoming obsolete...
What do LLMs struggle with? Language models achieve impressive performance in a variety of different applications, but they are not perfect. These models have known limitations, such as:
- Difficulty adding large numbers
- Inability to evaluate/solve complex equations
- Trouble with reasoning over iterative processes
For example, if we prompt an LLM with a description of the Fibonacci sequence then ask it to compute the 100th number, there is a high likelihood that it will fail! Why is this the case? Well, we know that LLMs struggle with performing arithmetic, and solving the Fibonacci sequence (unless the model uses brute force memorization) requires many, iterative additions between two numbers. If the model has a 95% chance of performing this addition correctly during each iteration, then the 100th Fibonacci number has a <1% chance of being correct!
What can we do to help? Typically, these limitations of LLMs were solved via prompting techniques like chain of thought (CoT) prompting or program of thoughts (PoT) prompting. CoT prompting uses few-shot learning to teach the language model how to output a problem-solving rationale along with its answer while solving any complex problem. Such an approach is found to drastically improve performance, especially on tasks that are reasoning-based. PoT prompting follows a similar approach, but also connects the model to an external code interpreter. Thus, the LLM can output a problem-solving program along with its chain of thought, which can then be executed to yield the final answer. The resulting system delegates problem-solving components to a program, which can more easily and reliably model concepts like basic arithmetic and iteration.
Is prompt engineering still necessary? CoT and PoT prompting work incredibly well, but it is unclear whether they are still necessary for powerful language models like GPT-4. For example, when we try to solve the Fibonacci sequence problem explained above, GPT-4 solves the problem effortlessly. Plus, GPT-4 seems to automatically generate a rationale along with its solution, even when we do not explicitly perform any CoT prompting! Given that GPT-4 has impressive coding capabilities, I wouldn’t be surprised if this model began to automatically adopt strategies similar to PoT prompting to solve complex problems in the future.
TL;DR: Cutting-edge language models are impressive and improving rapidly, which has made complex prompting techniques seem to be less necessary. Rather, models are learning to solve complex problems with less intricate prompts. These models are becoming more and more capable (literally) every day, so I’m sure prompting strategies and go-to approaches for using LLMs will continue to evolve.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Given all of the different prompt engineering strategies that exist, crafting a useful/effective prompt for solving problems with a language model can be pretty daunting and difficult. Here’s the sequences of steps I typically take when performing prompt engineering or creating any form of LLM-based problem-solving system.
Start simple: Before doing anything complicated, I start by trying to solve my problem with a simple instruction prompt. If this works, there is no reason to try anything more complicated! I only add complexity based on need.
Ensure structure and clarity: If my initial, simple prompt doesn’t work well, my next step is to try tweaking the prompt using different types of wording and structures/formats. For example, indicators can be added to the prompt to provide more structure (e.g., the instruction and question portion of the prompt can be clearly delineated for better clarity). Similarly, the actual wording of the prompt can be tweaked to make the prompt as clear and direct as possible.
Add few-shot examples: If you can’t get good results by simple format and wording tweaks, the next step should be adding few-shot exemplars to the prompt. How do you curate these examples? Typically, as I am evaluating prompt versions, I keep a set of problems/examples handy that I am trying to solve (basically a simple benchmark to determine if the LLM is solving the specified task or not). To find few-shot examples, I just use example tasks that the LLM fails to solve as I refine the prompt. Although this approach isn’t comprehensive, it’s a simple strategy that can be followed by a single person. By accruing more useful examples of proper LLM behavior over time, I find this simple strategy to be pretty effective.
What next? If few-shot learning does not work, there are two basic options that we have next: fine-tuning or complex prompting strategies. In general, fine-tuning (although it makes the resulting model more task-specific and less generic) is an extremely effective approach for teaching an LLM to solve a specific problem. Beating the performance of fine-tuning via in-context/few-shot learning is pretty difficult. If for whatever reason we can’t perform fine-tuning (e.g., if we are using the OpenAI API), then we should instead start to explore more complex prompting strategies (e.g., Chain of Thought prompting).
Making sure your prompt actually works: Sometimes, coming up with test cases on your own to test whether your prompts are working well is not enough. As a result, I typically provide access to the system that I am building to others on my team to try to “break” it after I’ve got it working pretty well. Typically, doing this will provide many more failure cases that you can use to further debug the LLM and improve your prompting strategy.
TL;DR: Prompt engineering can be complicated and there are a lot of options that can be used. To arrive at the best and most reliable results, start with an extremely simple prompt and add complexity only if the LLM is failing to accomplish your desired task. Start by modifying the wording and structure of your prompt, add few-shot examples if this doesn’t work, and only adopt complex prompting or fine-tuning strategies if none of these options solve your problems.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/FyRoZOqXwAIT1xw.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Connecting language models with tools can solve a lot of their limitations, but what do we do when the model doesn’t have access to a needed tool? Recent research indicates that modern language models (e.g., GPT-4) are capable of dynamically creating their own tools, forming a closed-loop system that can address its own needs when solving a problem.
Quick Analogy: This approach of allowing LLMs to create their own tools draws an interesting analogy to human life. Namely, the ability to fabricate our own tools led to major technological advancements within the human race. With this recent research, we are (at a higher and less rigorous level) testing whether the same is true of LLMs.
“According to the lessons learned from the evolutionary milestones of humans, a crucial turning point was that humans got the ability to fabricate their own tools to address emerging challenges. We embark on an initial exploration to apply this evolutionary concept to the realm of LLMs.” - from LaTM paper
Teaching LLMs to make their own tools: Teaching LLMs to use their own tools was explored by the LLMs as Tool Makers (LaTM) framework. Interaction with tools occurs in two phases: creation and usage. During creation, we use a few-shot learning approach to get the LLM to generate a needed tool (in the form of a Python function) based on examples of desired functionality. After the tool has been created (and passes functionality tests), we can prompt the LLM to use this tool by providing a description and usage examples.
Decoupling tool creation and usage: Notably, we do not have to use the same LLM for tool usage and creation. In most cases, it actually makes sense to use a more powerful LLM (e.g., GPT-4) for tool creation because it is a more difficult task. Then, we can save costs by adopting a more efficient LLM (e.g., GPT-3.5-turbo) for using these tools over time. Tool creation only occurs once, and we can re-use created tools as many times as is needed.
Making this more dynamic: If we want to dynamically identify the need for a new tool while solving a problem, we can just add an extra dispatcher agent to this system. The dispatcher simply decides whether to invoke an existing tool or create a new one given a current plan to solve a problem. This dispatcher is found to be ~95% accurate (even with smaller LLMs) when deciding between using existing or new tools.
TL;DR: Existing tool-usage approaches for LLMs rely on humans to curate a fixed set of useful tools. Recent research aims to make this system more dynamic by allowing LLMs to create and use their own tools. This approach is found to work relatively well, assuming that powerful LLMs (e.g., GPT-4 are used for tool creation).
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/FycpncoWcAIvMvM.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
In the wake of LLaMA, the deep learning research community quickly adopted the view that open-source LLMs will rule the future—reproducing open-source variants of proprietary models seemed to be easy and cheap. Is this the truth? Here’s a brief timeline of model proposals and what we know…
LLaMA. The surge of open-source LLM publications started with the proposal of LLaMA, a suite of LLMs with sizes ranging from 7 billion to 65 billion parameters. Taking inspiration from Chinchilla, these LLMs are a bit smaller than their counterparts but are pre-trained extensively, allowing them to perform surprisingly well for their size (e.g., 13B model is comparable to GPT-3). Unlike closed-source models that are trained on a combination of public and proprietary data, LLaMA uses only publicly available data for pre-training, making it fully open-source and possible to replicate.
LLaMA leak. After its proposal and release for research purposes, LLaMA weights were leaked to the public on 4Chan. This leak led many in the research community to begin doing research with the model, leading to a ton of different publications and proposals that we briefly overview below. A majority of these techniques fine-tune LLaMA on dialogue from ChatGPT (i.e., imitation models) and claim to achieve comparable performance, creating the view that creating open-source replicas of models like ChatGPT is actually quite easy.
Alpaca is a fine-tuned version of the LLaMA-7B LLM. The fine-tuning process is based on self-instruct, in which instruction-following data is collected from a higher-performing LLM (i.e., text-davinci-003) and used for supervised fine-tuning. The entire fine-tuning process of Alpaca costs only $600 (including both data collection and fine-tuning).
Vicuna is an open-source chatbot that is created by fine-tuning LLaMA-13B (i.e., comparable performance to GPT-3). Vicuna is fine-tuned using examples of user conversations with ChatGPT, and the entire fine-tuning process can be replicated for <$300, making chatbots more accessible for research purposes. Compared to Alpaca, Vicuna is more comparable to ChatGPT and generates answers with more detail and structure.
Koala is a version of LLaMA-13B that has been fine-tuned on dialogue data from a variety of sources, ranging from public datasets to dialogues with other high-quality LLMs that are available on the internet. Compared to Alpaca, Koala is fine-tuned over dialogue data and evaluated more extensively (using a larger number of crown workers).
GPT4ALL is a fine-tuned LLaMA-7B model that has been trained on over 800K chat completions from GPT-3.5-turbo. Along with releasing the code and model, authors of GPT4ALL release the 4-bit quantized weights of the model, which can be used to run inference on CPUs. The result is that we can actually host this model locally on a normal laptop.
Massive Potential. The models mentioned above were all published in close succession and (in most cases) claimed to achieve results that were comparable to top models like ChatGPT or GPT-4. As a result, the LLM community quickly adopted the opinion that open-source LLMs will soon match the quality of the most powerful proprietary models.
The Truth. When more targeted evaluations of these models is performed, we see that their performance is not as impressive as it seems. In reality, these models are good at matching the style and structure of models like ChatGPT when fine-tuned over a small amount of imitation data, but they lack the same knowledge base. Imitation models hallucinate more and perform poorly when subjected to a broader number of natural language benchmarks. Despite their limitations, these models were able to “trick” human evaluators via their style, despite being significantly less factual.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Next-token prediction is the workhorse behind all modern advancements in large language models (LLMs) due to its use in training these models over unlabeled text. But, how exactly does this next-token prediction (or language modeling) objective work? Let’s take a deeper look…
the basics. The next-token prediction objective is used for training LLMs in a self-supervised manner. Put simply, this means that we repeatedly perform the following two steps:
1. Sample some text from the dataset
2. Train the model to predict the token that comes after each token within the sampled text
This objective is self-supervised because we have access to an entire corpus of text. Thus, the ground truth next token is always known! No explicit labeling (e.g., from human annotators) is required to obtain this.
decoder-only transformers. LLMs use decoder-only transformers as their underlying architecture. The representation formed by this model for each token within a sequence depends only upon the tokens that precede it. As such, we can independently (and in parallel) predict the next token for all tokens within a sequence by just:
- Passing the sequence of tokens through all layers of the decoder-only transformer model
- Considering the final output embedding for each token within the sequence
- Treating next-token prediction as a classification problem over all tokens in our vocabulary that takes the current token's embedding as input
We can apply the next-token prediction loss over the entire sequence that has been passed through a decoder-only transformer and train the LLM using (stochastic) gradient descent!
next-token prediction in math. Consider a sequence of tokens given by U = [u1, u2, …]. Given a decoder-only transformer with parameters theta, the language modeling objective tries to maximize the conditional probability of a token given preceding tokens (see image for full expression). In other words, we maximize the probability of the model predicting the correct next token, given preceding tokens as context!
performing inference. We now understand the next-token prediction objective, but how does this teach an LLM to output coherent sequences of text? Well, generating text is just next-token prediction! We can just follow the steps below:
- Consider a current sequence of tokens
- Generate the next token using the LLM
- Append this token to the sequence
- Repeat
This autoregressive process is called “decoding” within the LLM community, and there are several different types of decoding we can perform (e.g., greedy decoding, nucleus sampling, etc.).
TL;DR: The next-token prediction (or language modeling) objective is a self-supervised objective that is used heavily by LLMs for both pre-training and (supervised) fine-tuning. It operates by trying to continually classify the token that comes after the current token within a sequence of text, and we can apply it over an entire sequence of tokens at once (i.e., with a single forward pass) during training due to the use of a decoder-only transformer. Because it also mimics the decoding procedure used to generate text, next-token prediction is a fitting and efficient objective for training LLMs.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The LLaMA suite of large language models (LLMs) led to a surge in publications on the topic of open-source LLMs. Many of these works adopted an imitation approach, in which less powerful LLMs were fine-tuned on ChatGPT dialogues. These imitation models seemed to perform comparably to ChatGPT at first, but the full story is a bit more complicated.
What is model imitation? Model imitation is based upon the more generic idea of knowledge distillation and is a (seemingly) effective way to fine-tune less powerful LLMs to quickly make them much better at following instructions. To do this, we just:
- Collect dialogue examples from the more powerful model (e.g., using the OpenAI API).
- Use them to fine-tune the smaller model using a normal language modeling objective.
This approach is not commercially viable (i.e., see OpenAI API’s terms and conditions), but it was used to create models like Alpaca, Vicuna, Koala, and GPT4All.
The open-source LLM movement. Several different imitation models were published in close succession following the release of LLaMA. In many cases, these models claimed to achieve results that were comparable to top proprietary models like ChatGPT or GPT-4. As such, the research community quickly adopted the opinion that open-source models will soon dominate the LLM landscape.
“Open-source models are faster, more customizable, more private, and … more capable. They are doing things with $100 and 13B params that [Google] struggles with at $10M and 540B. And they are doing so in weeks, not months.” - from
Are imitation models actually performant? Although it seemed like the pace and trajectory of research on open-source LLMs would soon lead proprietary models to become less desirable, the story is not quite this simple. Most of these imitation models were evaluated minimally and primarily by using crowd workers. Going further, evaluation using crowd workers can be misleading, as LLMs that match the style of ChatGPT can typically score well, even if they lack the same knowledge base and factuality. Put simply, LLMs with convincing style can score well even if they output incorrect information. Investigating whether an LLM’s information is correct requires a significant time investment, leading hallucinations to be overlooked by crowd workers in certain cases.
The (unfortunate) truth. In “The False Promise of Imitating Proprietary LLMs”, authors rigorously benchmark a variety of imitation models, attempting to teach open-source models to mimic ChatGPT both on specific tasks and in general. Interestingly, these models are found to perform much worse than ChatGPT (and even the base LLM) when subjected to broader and more rigorous evaluations. While these models can accurately imitate the behavior of a powerful model on specific tasks (i.e., local imitation), teaching such models to perform comparably to ChatGPT in general (i.e., broad imitation) would require a massive dataset of imitation examples that is difficult to curate. As such, imitation models tend to only perform well on tasks that are well-represented in their fine-tuning datasets.
TL;DR: Numerous imitation models were proposed in quick succession and made it seem like open-source LLMs were taking over, but this is not the case (yet). These models have major limitations that were overlooked due to a lack of rigor in evaluation. Nonetheless, the open-source LLM movement is still very much alive and progressing! Imitation models are just one idea in this very promising area.

summary:
When we interact with language model APIs, such as the OpenAI API, we typically have to set a “temperature” parameter when obtaining output from the language model. But, what exactly is this parameter and how does it work? Let’s take a deeper look…
The decoding process: Inference with a language model is performed via an autoregressive decoding process. This sounds complicated, but the process is pretty simple. Given a sequence of input tokens, we just:
- Use the language model to predict the next token
- Add this output token to our input sequence
- Repeat
By continually generating the next token in this manner (i.e., this is what we call the autoregressive decoding process), we can generate an entire textual sequence. But, how do we use the language model to determine what the next token should be?
Token probabilities: Language models do not output an actual token. Rather, they output a probability distribution over all possible tokens that are known by the model. This set of potential tokens is referred to as the Vocabulary, which typically contains ~100K-1M unique tokens. Given this probability distribution, there are several decoding strategies that we can follow, which are just different ways of selecting the next token from this distribution. For example a “greedy” decoding strategy repeatedly selects the token with the highest probability. See my prior tweet (in the replies) for more details.
What does temperature do? Different values of the temperature simply impact our decoding strategy, changing the way in which we iteratively select the next token. Stated intuitively, higher values of temperature make output more random, while lower values of temperature make output more deterministic (e.g., using a temperature of 0 will output the same/similar sequence every time).
More details: The language model’s probability distribution over tokens is formed with a softmax transformation, which transforms logits produced by the language model into a valid probability distribution. Temperature is simply a hyperparameter within this softmax transformation (see image for equations). Higher values of this temperature result in a more uniform distribution over tokens, while lower values of temperature create a distribution that assigns high probability to a single token. Thus, temperature simply modifies the distribution according to which we sample tokens!
A word of caution: Temperature can help us with generating more diverse outputs with a language model. But, it also increases the chance of the model generating something random or irrelevant. Thus, we should use higher values of temperature with caution!

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The temperature setting is a numerical "lever" that controls the randomness of an LLM's decoding process. Low temperature yields a more deterministic output and vice versa. But, setting your temperature to zero does NOT mean the LLM's output will always be the same! Here's why...
decoding discrepancies. When the LLM is used to compute the probability distribution over potential next tokens, numerical instabilities/discrepancies may occur in this process. This means that even if we are using a greedy decoding strategy (i.e., always pick the highest-probability next token), slight deviations in floating point operations could lead the next token that is produced to be different between calls.
it only takes one token. If one token in the output is different, it is easy to see that the entire decoding process following that token is completely changed! We now have a different sequence and the distribution over potential next tokens will not be the same. Thus, a difference of a single token causes the entire decoding process to diverge afterwards.
TL;DR: Temperature does control how deterministic an LLM's output is, as described in the tweet below. But, small numerical discrepancies between forward passes can cause deviations in the output, even if we have a temperature of 0. With this in mind, there is currently no way to ensure that an LLM's output will always be the same for a given input.
Quoting @cwolferesearch
When we interact with language model APIs, such as the OpenAI API, we typically have to set a “temperature” parameter when obtaining output from the language model. But, what exactly is this parameter and how does it work? Let’s take a deeper look…
The decoding process: Inference with a language model is performed via an autoregressive decoding process. This sounds complicated, but the process is pretty simple. Given a sequence of input tokens, we just:
- Use the language model to predict the next token
- Add this output token to our input sequence
- Repeat
By continually generating the next token in this manner (i.e., this is what we call the autoregressive decoding process), we can generate an entire textual sequence. But, how do we use the language model to determine what the next token should be?
Token probabilities: Language models do not output an actual token. Rather, they output a probability distribution over all possible tokens that are known by the model. This set of potential tokens is referred to as the Vocabulary, which typically contains ~100K-1M unique tokens. Given this probability distribution, there are several decoding strategies that we can follow, which are just different ways of selecting the next token from this distribution. For example a “greedy” decoding strategy repeatedly selects the token with the highest probability. See my prior tweet (in the replies) for more details.
What does temperature do? Different values of the temperature simply impact our decoding strategy, changing the way in which we iteratively select the next token. Stated intuitively, higher values of temperature make output more random, while lower values of temperature make output more deterministic (e.g., using a temperature of 0 will output the same/similar sequence every time).
More details: The language model’s probability distribution over tokens is formed with a softmax transformation, which transforms logits produced by the language model into a valid probability distribution. Temperature is simply a hyperparameter within this softmax transformation (see image for equations). Higher values of this temperature result in a more uniform distribution over tokens, while lower values of temperature create a distribution that assigns high probability to a single token. Thus, temperature simply modifies the distribution according to which we sample tokens!
A word of caution: Temperature can help us with generating more diverse outputs with a language model. But, it also increases the chance of the model generating something random or irrelevant. Thus, we should use higher values of temperature with caution!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/FzLQ7G9WAAQ221S.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
To achieve maximum throughput when training a language model, we need to use large batches and long sequences of text. How can we construct optimally-sized batches of data for training a language model? Just use the packing technique!
Background: When we train a language model, training is performed using stochastic gradient descent iterations over a “mini-batch” of textual sequences. Each sequence in this mini-batch has a maximum length (e.g., 2,048 tokens). If a sequence of text that we are using for training the language model is shorter than this maximum length, we add “padding tokens” to this sequence to ensure that all inputs in the mini-batch have the same size.
Padding is problematic: Although padding is great for adding structure to a mini-batch (i.e., it makes sure all sequences have the same length), it also wastes a lot of compute. The language model has to perform computation over these padding tokens that ultimately will not be used for anything!
“We show in this paper that the variation in sequence lengths in common NLP datasets is such that up to 50% of all tokens can be padding.” - from Efficient Sequence Packing without Cross-Contamination
The solution: Packing is a quick trick that minimizes the number of padding tokens by just concatenating multiple text sequences into a single example within a mini-batch. Then, the total length of the resulting sequence is much closer to the desired/maximum sequence length, allowing fewer padding tokens to be used. Practically, this is done by shuffling input examples and partitioning them into groups such that the total length of each concatenated sequence does not exceed the maximum sequence length. This problem is related to the famous bin packing problem in computer science and can be solved using a variety of different heuristic approximations.
Further reading: The packing technique is proposed and analyzed in “Efficient Sequence Packing without Cross-contamination”. In addition to proposing this useful trick, the paper holds a lot of valuable insights regarding the quality and properties of data used for language model pre-training, as well as how to train a language model as efficiently as possible!

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Can large language models (LLMs) train themselves? The explosion of imitation-based open-source LLMs drew criticism due to cursory evaluation that covered up performance gaps. However, recent research shows powerful open-source LLMs can actually be created by imitating other models.
Background: Although many popular LLMs are proprietary, there is a burgeoning movement in the LLM community to create powerful open-source models. Many open-source models have been proposed, but this movement was especially catalyzed by the recent proposal of LLaMA. Following the release of LLaMA, the research community created numerous derivates of the model that are fine-tuned via an imitation approach. In other words, we take dialogue examples from proprietary LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT) and directly fine-tune the open-source LLM (i.e., LLaMA) on this data.
Poor Evaluation: Initially, the evaluation of these imitation models indicated that they came near the performance of top proprietary LLMs. If true, this finding would mean that creating open-source replicas of proprietary LLMs is easy and cheap. However, subsequent research concluded that the evaluation of such models was incomplete and misleading, finding that these models actually have large gaps in their comprehension. These gaps in performance were missed in human evaluations due to the ability of imitation models to replicate the style of LLMs like ChatGPT (but not their reasoning and knowledge base).
“Our research indicates that learning from step-by-step explanations, whether these are generated by humans or more advanced AI models, is a promising direction to improve model capabilities and skills.” - from Orca paper
Orca: Recently, however, the Orca publication (from Microsoft) showed us that imitation learning is not a dead end! Put simply, the problem with existing imitation models is that their fine-tuning dataset is too small/narrow and does not contain sufficient details from the “teacher” model. By creating a better imitation fine-tuning dataset, Orca is able to achieve performance comparable to ChatGPT across a wide scope of standardized benchmarks.
How do we do this? Prior imitation models are trained over pairs of prompts and associated responses generated from an LLM. This information is shallow and lacks details regarding why/how a response was produced. To generate more detailed data, Orca prompts the teacher model to output a detailed explanation along with its normal response. Drawing upon ideas like zero-shot CoT prompting, we can encourage the model to produce detailed explanations with each of its responses by just tweaking the system message. Then, we can fine-tune the imitation model using both the response and the explanation as a training signal.
TL;DR: Orca proposes a much larger (6M examples from ChatGPT and GPT-4) imitation fine-tuning dataset that is augmented with step-by-step problem-solving details for each of a model’s responses. By fine-tuning LLaMA over this data, we get an open-source LLM that actually comes near the performance of ChatGPT. With this in mind, imitation is a valid approach for creating useful open-source LLMs given a much better source of fine-tuning data.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/FzkZtu8aEAAJWKM.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The MPT suite of large language models (LLMs) by MosaicML has become incredibly popular. But, what makes these models so special? Although there are a variety of reasons for the popularity of MPT, I find these models to be especially useful due to a few unique components…
Fully open-source. MPT models, including MPT-7B and MPT-30B, carry an Apache 2.0 license, meaning that they can be used commercially without any limitations. Plus, these models are accompanied by an entire open-source code repository for fine-tuning, evaluating, or even pre-training these models from scratch (see replies for more details). Given that pre-training a base LLM is the most prohibitive/expensive component of any LLM-based system, the MPT foundation series is a great starting point for building specialized LLMs that solve domain-specific problems.
Fast inference. MPT models are based upon a typical, decoder-only transformer architecture. But, they make a few key modifications to this architecture, including:
- Low precision layer norm
- Flash Attention
- ALiBi (instead of normal positional embeddings)
Due to these modifications, MPT models perform inference very quickly (i.e., 1.5-2X faster than similarly-sized LLaMA models) with HuggingFace inference pipelines. Plus, MPT models are completely compatible with libraries like FasterTransformer, which could be used to further boost inference speed.
Context length. Due to their use of ALiBi, MPT-7B and 30B are capable of handling large context windows and can even extrapolate to context lengths that are beyond data seen during training. To show this, MPT-7B is fine-tuned on data with a 64K token context length (derived from books3 corpus of fiction novels). Researchers at MosaicML found that this MPT-StoryWriter-7B model was capable of handling large context lengths and could even extrapolate further to context windows as large as 84K. They even ingested the entire Great Gatsby book and generated an epilogue!
Performance. Finally, MPT models perform really well. MPT-7B achieves performance on-par with LLaMA-7B across a variety of standard benchmarks. MPT-30B lags slightly behind the performance of LLaMA-30B and Falcon-40B on text-based tasks, but it tends to perform better on programming tasks. Plus, MPT-30B seems to exceed the quality of GPT-3. Put simply, these base models are high-quality and serve as a great foundation for creating open-source alternatives to proprietary systems like ChatGPT or GPT-4.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/FzvPmCZXoAADvoC.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Recent research on language models has aimed to increase the maximum allowable context length of the underlying model. But, how can we enable an LLM to handle longer inputs? One way is through the use of ALiBi…
Vanilla position embeddings. Decoder-only transformer architectures create an input sequence of tokens by first tokenizing the raw text and looking up the embedding (each token in the tokenizer’s vocabulary has a unique embedding) for each token. Then, we add a positional embedding to each token embedding, which injects positional info into the embedding of each token in the sequence.
Why is this necessary? We should recall that the self-attention operation is agnostic to the position of a token in a sequence! The only way to consider the position of each token when computing self-attention is to inject such information into each token’s embedding or into the attention computation itself.
ALiBi > position embeddings. Attention with Linear Biases (ALiBi) gets rid of positional embeddings altogether. Instead, positional information is injected into the transformer as part of the self-attention operation via adding a penalty to the key-query attention score. In particular, we should recall that self-attention computes an attention score between each pair of tokens within a sequence. ALiBi operates by adding a static, non-learned bias to this score that is proportional to the distance between the pair of tokens.
The result. Such an approach is impactful because it depends on the pairwise distance between tokens rather than the absolute positions of tokens within a sequence. This quantity is less dependent upon the length of the underlying sequence and allows ALiBi to generalize much better to sequences that are longer than those seen during training. For example, MPT-7B (which uses ALiBi) can be fine-tuned on sequences as long as 64K and reasonably extrapolate to much longer sequences of 84K tokens.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Fz5DkCgWABc22uh.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The foundation series by MosaicML, including MPT-7B/30B (and an efficient training repo), makes high-quality pre-trained language models available to anyone for commercial use. Given that creating a pre-trained base model is incredibly expensive, these open-source tools enable a wide variety of specialized language model use cases to be explored at a reduced cost.
Some background. All language models are created using a common framework with a few simple components, including pre-training, refinement (SFT and RLHF), and application. Although this framework has several steps, the first step (pre-training) is arguably the most important. Creating a more powerful base model via extensive, high-quality pre-training enables better results when the LLM is refined and applied. Put simply, the base model is a common starting point for all LLM applications, so improving the base model benefits the entire application.
Open-source base LLMs. Until recently, open-source base models either performed poorly (e.g., OPT or BLOOM) compared to their proprietary counterparts or could only be used for research (e.g., LLaMA). This changed with the release of MPT-7B and MPT-30B by MosaicML, which are open-source, performant, and commercially usable. Plus, these models can be fine-tuned (at a low cost) using MosaicML’s LLM foundry, allowing AI practitioners to easily specialize these models to a variety of different use cases.
What makes these models so good? There are a variety of factors that make MPT-7B/30B impressive, but the most notable considerations are enumerated below.
- Use of the GPT-NeoX tokenizer (better handles whitespace for code)
- Pre-trained over a lot of data (1T tokens in total)
- Use of a modified architecture (low precision layer norm, flash attention, ALiBi, and more) that enables faster training/inference and extrapolation to long context lengths
- MPT-7B is fine-tuned with context lengths as large as 64K tokens
- MPT-30B base model is trained using a longer context length of 8K tokens (compared to 2K for most open-source LLMs)
- MPT-30B places an emphasis on code in its pre-training data, making the resulting LLM especially good at coding applications
MPT performance. MPT models are evaluated extensively and compared to other popular, open-source LLMs. MPT-7B is found to be comparable to LLaMA-7B, and both of these models are significantly better than any prior open-source LLM of this size. MPT-30B achieves comparable performance to GPT-3. It is outperformed by models like LLaMA-30B and Falcon-40B on text-based tasks but tends to excel in code-based tasks.
TL;DR: The foundation models provided by MosaicML are a huge step forward for the open-source LLM community, as they provide commercially-usable LLMs that are comparable to popular base models like LLaMA and GPT-3. The MPT-7B and 30B models come with an entire ecosystem of open-source tools that can be used to create specialized/personalized LLMs, thus providing a starting point for solving a variety of downstream applications.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
When querying a language model, there are many ways to tweak the randomness of the model’s generations. One popular method is via the “top_k” setting, which works in tandem with the temperature parameter to increase the diversity of generated text. Here's how this works...
Autoregressive decoding. Inference with a language model is performed via an autoregressive decoding process that:
- Considers a sequence of tokens as input
- Uses the language model to predict the next token
- Adds this output token to the input sequence
- Repeats
Here, the word “autoregressive” refers to the fact that we add each output token as part of our input for the next step. By continually generating tokens in this manner, we can generate an entire textual sequence.
Distribution over tokens. The output of a language model in each of the autoregressive decoding steps is a probability distribution over all possible tokens that are known by the model. Given this probability distribution, there are several decoding strategies that we can follow, which are just different ways of selecting the next token to output from this distribution. For example a “greedy” decoding strategy repeatedly selects the token with the highest probability. Alternatively, we could just sample randomly from this distribution, where tokens with higher probability are sampled more frequently.
top_k setting. The setting of top_k impacts the decoding process by transforming the distribution over tokens. Instead of sampling randomly from the resulting distribution during decoding, we select the top_k highest probability tokens within the distribution and redistribute the probability mass over these tokens such that the summed probability over the top_k tokens is equal to 1 (i.e., just normalize the distribution over the top_k tokens). For example, top_k=3 would redistribute token probabilities over the three highest-probability tokens within the distribution. Then, we perform decoding by sampling randomly from this distribution of top_k tokens!
Practical impact. The resulting setting of top_k allows the randomness of the model’s output to be controlled, similar to the temperature or top_p settings. If we choose a larger value of top_k, then the model is allowed to select from a larger number of potential tokens during decoding. Selecting a single token differently changes the entire decoding process that follows. As such, increasing the value of top_k can result in a larger diversity of generated sequences and vice versa.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Given the current foundation model paradigm, I wonder if building/training models will become antiquated. Will future data scientists understand the details of optimization, architectures, etc.? ML may slowly be abstracted in favor of simpler (language model-based) solutions...
Some background. When I first got started in machine/deep learning, PyTorch did not yet exist. Implementing back propagation from scratch was relatively common (I was even asked to do this on the spot in an interview!) and doing any deep learning-related research required a significant amount of boilerplate programming. Today, most of the fundamental knowledge required for deep learning (e.g., back propagation, weight initialization, model architectures, etc.) is already abstracted significantly by packages like PyTorch and HuggingFace. Most of the time, we don't think much about these details, choosing instead to use default settings or implementations provided by our framework of choice.
Training from scratch is (relatively) uncommon. For the first few years of my career, training machine learning models from scratch was standard. I implemented countless training pipelines for a variety of different models (e.g., regression, random forests, MLPs, RNNs, …). Since the proposal of BERT in 2018, I have used pre-trained transformer models (sometimes with added components based on pre-trained CNNs) for pretty much everything that I do. The variety of different model types that I’ve used throughout my years have been replaced by a few common transformer architectures. Plus, I don’t even implement these architectures myself! I simply download a pre-trained model, fine-tune it on whatever task I’m interested in, and deploy. I have not truly trained/created a model “from scratch” in quite a while.
Should you implement training yourself? Even after learning to rely heavily upon pre-trained model architectures and weights, I continued to implement my own fine-tuning code or training loop when using these models. Recently, however, writing your own training loop has become less and less common. In fact, given the widespread availability of optimized training frameworks, implementing your own training code might even be a bad idea! Although PyTorch’s zero_grad(); backward(); step() cadence will be burned into my memory forever, it is now much more efficient to leverage the optimized Trainer classes offered by packages like PyTorch Lightning, MosaicML composer, or other alternatives.
Everything keeps getting abstracted! Put simply, the research community has abstracted away a lot of complications associated with deep learning over time. Currently, model architectures, training loops (including all the details of optimization), pre-trained weights (and weight initializations), and more are all handled via a simple setting within a deep learning package. By examining this trend towards abstracting everything in the lens of the growing popularity of LLMs, we have to ask: where/when will this abstraction end?
Some considerations. At this point, there are a few common points that most will make to argue against using language models for everything. E.g., inference is expensive, the models are large and difficult to host at scale, fine-tuned models still perform better, etc. Although these points are completely valid, I would also argue the following:
- LLM inference speed is improving quickly due to advancements like FlashAttention, parallel transformer blocks, and low precision modules.
- Hosting these models has been democratized significantly due to advancements in quantization (and this will probably continue to improve moving forward).
- In practice, implementing any machine/deep learning system is a tradeoff between complexity and performance.
In many cases, companies will prefer a model that can be implemented in 1 day over a slightly higher-performing model that takes several weeks/months to develop. The simple text-to-text interface of language models is (in my opinion) heavily underestimated. It can be leveraged by someone with minimal (or no) ML-related knowledge to quickly solve tasks that would’ve previously required entire teams of data scientists.
Looking forward. With all this being said, I’m not sure how the day-to-day roles of machine learning engineers and data scientists will change moving forward. In my opinion, there is still incredible value in expert knowledge of machine learning fundamentals. However, I believe that the current generations of ML practitioners might find that they use this knowledge less and less over time, just as how my detailed knowledge of back propagation, weight initialization schemes, transformer architecture variants, etc. no longer serves an impactful/practical purpose in my current day-to-day life.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The recently-proposed Falcon-40B model achieves unprecedented levels of performance in comparison to other open-source large language models (LLMs) and even rivals the quality of paid models. Here are the key attributes of Falcon-40B that contribute most to its success…
More data from the web. Many LLMs are pre-trained over curated text corpora (e.g., C4 or The Pile), but creating these curated data sources is not scalable. To efficiently obtain lots of high-quality pre-training data, authors of Falcon create a massive (5T tokens in total, but only ~1T tokens are used) textual corpus, called RefinedWeb, by applying simple/efficient filtering rules to a large amount of web data from CommonCrawl.
Curated data still helps. Although models trained solely on RefinedWeb data perform well (i.e., better than those trained only on curated data), Falcon-40B is pre-trained on 1 trillion tokens from RefinedWeb combined with a smaller amount of curated data from the Pile. This combination of curated and large-scale web data yields a pre-training corpus that is both large and of high quality.
Fast inference. The Falcon-40B model uses a modified decoder-only architecture that is optimized for fast inference. In particular, the model uses:
- Flash Attention
- Multi-Query Attention
- Parallel Attention and Feed Forward Layers
As a result, Falcon-40B can perform inference over 5X faster than GPT-3 and can even be pre-trained more efficiently than popular models like PaLM-62B and Chinchilla.
Context windows. One of the main limitations of Falcon-40B is that it is trained using a sequence length of 2K, which is arguably small compared to many recent models (e.g., MPT or Claude). However, the use of RoPE embeddings within Falcon-40B’s architecture theoretically allows the model to generalize to longer sequence lengths (though this might work better after some fine-tuning).

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Curriculum learning has been recently become an impactful technique for training LLMs. But, did you know that this idea has existed in the AI community for nearly 15 years? The models being trained have changed, but the core idea remains incredibly valuable…
What is curriculum learning? When we train a neural network, we typically perform several training epochs over a fixed dataset using (mini-batch) stochastic gradient descent. Instead, curriculum (or progressive) learning devises a strategy/curriculum for exposing this data to our model (e.g., smaller images first, then larger images later). This idea is incredibly generic and can take many different forms in practice.
Application to LLMs. Interestingly, curriculum learning has recently become heavily used for training LLMs, and several papers have reported improved results from adopting a training curriculum. Let’s take a look at a few notable examples to make things more concrete.
1. Orca
Orca is a derivative of LLaMA that is fine-tuned on dialogues from proprietary LLMs. Orca’s fine-tuning procedure first trains on 5 million dialogues from ChatGPT, then finishes fine-tuning with 1M dialogues from GPT-4. Not only does Orca perform incredibly well, but the authors claim that this progressive fine-tuning approach benefits performance.
2. MPT-30B
MPT-30B is a commercially-licensed, open-source LLM from MosaicML. MPT-30B has an 8K context length. However, the pre-training procedure uses a 2K context length at first, then finishes with an 8K context length. This curriculum is found to benefit efficiency while still yielding a model with a larger context window.
Proposal in 2009! Although curriculum learning has been successfully applied in recent research on LLMs, the idea dates all the way back to a paper called “Curriculum Learning” (by Yoshua Bengio) that was published in 2009 at ICML. Although reading recent papers is fun and exciting, we should always recall that revisiting older/established papers can lead to ideas that are equally valuable!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F03Kg6IWYAIyUdz.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Recently proposed open-source language models have placed an emphasis upon inference speed. Such work has shown us that inference speed can be improved by up to 5X (or more) by making some changes to the decoder-only transformer architecture. Here are three examples that have appeared frequently in recent work…
1. Flash attention: Self-attention is an O(N^2) operation, where N is the input length. Many efficient attention implementations (e.g., Reformer or Performer) have O(N) complexity but achieve minimal wall clock speedup due to IO latency. Flash attention solves this problem by reformulating attention in an efficient and IO-aware manner.
2. Multi-query attention: Multi-query attention shares key and value vectors between all attention head in a layer instead of performing a separate projection for each head. Although this change does not make training any faster, it significantly improves the inference speed of the resulting LLM.
3. Parallel layers: Most transformer architectures use a “serial” structure in each block. Alternatively, we can perform self-attention and the feed-forward transformation in parallel, followed by a single layer norm operation. This formulation does not deteriorate performance and can improve inference speed by parallelizing major operations in a transformer layer.
The impact: All three of the above modifications are added to the architecture of the recently-proposed Falcon-40B model. As a result, Falcon-40B can perform inference 5X faster than GPT-3 and even requires less compute for pre-training compared to comparable models like PaLM-62B or Chinchilla.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
FlashAttention-2 was released today, which is 5-9X faster than vanilla attention and 2X faster than FlashAttention-v1. Given that many of the top open-source LLMs leverage FlashAttention, this is an important advancement that can make existing models much more efficient during both training and inference. Here’s what you need to know…
What is FlashAttention? In its canonical form, self-attention is an O(N^2) operation, where N is the length of the input sequence. Many proposals try to achieve an approximation of self-attention that runs in O(N) time, but they achieve no wall-clock speedup. FlashAttention reformulates attention in an IO-aware manner to achieve significant wall clock speedups, as well as an improvement in memory efficiency.
Lots of LLMs use it. Given that FlashAttention is very fast (i.e., ~2-4X faster) compared to a vanilla implementation, many transformer-based applications have adopted it. For example, recent open-source LLMs (such as Falcon and MPT models) use FlashAttention, leading them to be very fast at inference time (and more efficient during pre-training). For example, Falcon-40B is 5X faster at performing inference than GPT-3.
FlashAttention-2. A new update to FlashAttention has just been made available, called FlashAttention-2. This variant is about twice as fast as the original FlashAttention, and 5-9X faster than the original attention implementation. This improvement impacts both training an inference speed. The sources of these improvements are summarized by the quote below.
“We (1) tweak the algorithm to reduce the number of non-matmul FLOPs (2) parallelize the attention computation, even for a single head, across different thread blocks to increase occupancy, and (3) within each thread block, distribute the work between warps to reduce communication through shared memory.” - from FlashAttention-2 paper
The only caveat. Currently, the FlashAttention-2 implementation does not apply to all GPUs. However, the GPUs to which it does apply see a significant benefit; e.g., a 225 TFLOPs/s training speed can be achieved on an A100 using FlashAttention-2.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The ability to perform high-quality alignment led to a massive breakthrough in the quality of language models. Although many proprietary models dedicate extensive human/compute resources to aligning base LLMs, recent research indicates that we can align language models with significantly less effort. We just need to make sure that our data is good enough…
LLM training pipeline: Training a language model has as few standard steps. First, we pre-train the model on unlabeled text. Then, we align the model using SFT (fine-tuning over good responses) and/or RLHF (learning from human feedback via RL). Finally, we deploy our model and use either extra fine-tuning or in-context learning to guarantee the best results.
What is alignment? Alignment drastically improves language model quality by teaching the model to generate outputs that align with the preferences of a human user. Recent research indicates that alignment serves to teach the language model the correct output format and style. Notably, the model does not seem to learn new information during alignment.
LIMA: The problem of alignment was studied by the recent LIMA model, where we see that high-quality alignment can be performed via SFT with a dataset of only 1,000 highly-curated examples. Put simply, this work reveals that alignment can be learned with very few data examples, a phenomenon that is called the “Superficial Alignment Hypothesis”.
The key to alignment: Although we don’t need a ton of data for alignment, the data that is used must be high-quality and diverse. Authors of LIMA accomplish this by constructing an alignment dataset that: (1) adopts a uniform response tone/style, (2) uses diverse prompts, and (3) is manually curated to ensure quality. Interestingly, the scale of the alignment dataset alone does not impact model quality.
TL;DR: Alignment is incredibly important, and recent research indicates that alignment can be achieved via SFT on a small dataset of curated examples. Proprietary models invest significant resources into alignment, but we see in LIMA and beyond (e.g., Orca) that investing into the quality of alignment data (rather than scale) is highly beneficial.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Recent language models have heavily emphasized automatic collection of training data, either from other models or via frameworks like self-instruct. But, this approach is probably not optimal, as LLMs are not exempt from the “garbage in, garbage out” rule…
LLM training pipeline. Language models are trained in several stages. First, we have pre-training, where the model is trained using a language modeling objective on a massive textual corpus. Then, we align the model using SFT and/or RLHF. Both of these stages are reliant upon the curation of an associated training dataset.
Recent approaches. Especially for alignment, recent research initiatives have attempted to collect training datasets automatically. For example, Alpaca and Vicuna use conversations from proprietary models like ChatGPT (downloaded from the internet) as a training target. Additionally, most of the pre-training corpora used by popular LLMs are filtered using an ML-centric approach.
Quality > quantity. Although automatically curating data is more easy/efficient, the data used for training must also be high-quality and diverse. Scale of data alone provides minimal benefit to LLM performance. Having a lot of data is good, but we need high-quality data too!
The result. As proof that data quality matters, we see with the recent LIMA LLM that near state-of-the-art alignment results can be achieved via fine-tuning only only 1,000 prompt-response examples. These examples are manually curated to ensure diversity and quality. Such a result indicates that data quality directly impacts the effectiveness of alignment.
Beyond alignment. Although LIMA shows that data quality is important for alignment, this lesson applies elsewhere as well. For example, the recent Falcon LLM (state-of-the-art until LLaMA-2) invests significant effort into curating a clean and diverse pre-training set. Additionally, the diversity and quality of examples used in few-shot learning prompts drastically impacts model performance.
TL;DR: We can find numerous examples of data quality impacting results of LLM pre-training, alignment, in-context learning, and more. No matter the context, having data that is diverse and clean will yield a benefit to LLM performance!

When language models first gained recognition, most LLMs were only accessible via APIs. Although this seemed to be a new standard, the proposal of a few notable models created hope for open-source LLMs and shifted the evolution of research in this area…
“Academia, nonprofits and smaller companies' research labs find it difficult to create, study, or even use LLMs as only a few industrial labs with the necessary resources and exclusive rights can fully access them.” - from BLOOM paper
GPT-NeoX-20B (successor to GPT-Neo-2.7B) is a 20 billion parameter dense autoregressive language model that is pre-trained on the Pile. This model, despite being relatively small, performed comparably to proprietary LLMs like GPT-3 and was one of the largest open-source LLMs available at the time.
OPT is a suite of LLMs that contains one of the first truly large language models to be open-sourced (OPT-175B). Despite lagging behind proprietary models in terms of performance, OPT contains open-source models, code, and logbooks that provided invaluable insights and transparency into LLM research.
BLOOM is a 176 billion parameter LLM created as part of an open collaboration of over 1,000 AI researchers. This model can generate text in 46 natural languages and 13 programming languages. Interestingly, BLOOM was the first >1B parameter LLM to be trained on many of these languages.
Several other open-source LLMs exist that catalyzed research in this area, such as GPT-J and GLM. Plus, numerous high-quality, open-source LLMs have since been proposed: LLaMA, MPT, Falcon, and (most recently) LLaMA-2. Open-source LLMs are now a big research topic thanks to early initiatives like OPT and BLOOM!
The impact of these models was large despite their performance lagging behind proprietary counterparts. Their proposal came at a time when closed-source seemed to be a new standard. These early open-source LLMs shifted the direction of AI research by demonstrating the feasibility of training such massive models for research purposes.
“A much broader segment of the AI community needs access to these models in order to conduct reproducible research and collectively drive the field forward.” - from OPT paper
