summary:
LLaMA-2 outlines the remaining limitations of open-source language models well. Put simply, the gap in performance between open-source and proprietary LLMs is largely due to the quality of alignment. However, LLaMA-2 takes a major step in the right direction…
State of open-source LLMs. Many pre-trained, open-source LLMs have been released (e.g., BLOOM, LLaMA, and MPT). These models perform comparably to closed-source base models like GPT-3 or Chinchilla, but they fall behind the performance of top models like ChatGPT or GPT-4.
Why is closed-source better? Top proprietary models outperform open-source LLMS because they are highly-aligned. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have invested heavily into collecting fine-tuning data and human feedback for SFT/RLHF to make these models more steerable and effective.
“These closed product LLMs are heavily fine-tuned to align with human preferences, which greatly enhances their usability and safety. This step can require significant costs in compute and human annotation, and is often not transparent or easily reproducible…” - from LLaMA-2 paper
What are we waiting for? Performing high-quality alignment is expensive in terms of both compute and human resources. To avoid this cost, most open-source models are aligned via SFT on publicly-available datasets. Clearly, however, research on open-source LLMs needs to focus on higher-quality alignment to close the performance gap with proprietary models.
A step in the right direction. LLaMA-2, in addition to being pre-trained on a massive 2 trillion token corpus, is extensively aligned to improve dialogue capabilities. LLaMA-2 undergoes SFT on a custom-curated dataset of 100,000 dialogue examples and RLHF on a dataset of 1M human preferences.
“Llama 2-Chat is the result of several months of research and iterative applications of alignment techniques, including both instruction tuning and RLHF, requiring significant computational and annotation resources” - from LLaMA-2 paper
Fine-tuning data. LLaMA-2 first undergoes SFT with public datasets. However, this data is found to lack in quality/diversity, so the authors curate a higher-quality dataset of 27,540 prompt-response pairs, which massively improves performance. Fewer but higher-quality examples is better.
RLHF annotation. Data for RLHF is collected by i) asking human annotators to write a prompt, ii) sampling two model responses to the prompt, and iii) having human annotators select the better response. Over 1M pieces of human feedback are sampled in this manner and used to train LLaMA via RLHF.
The result of LLaMA-2’s extensive alignment efforts is a model that far outperforms existing open-source LLMs, including top models like MPT-30B and Falcon-40B. Additionally, LLaMA-2-Chat even performs comparably to models like ChatGPT in human trials. The better alignment approach produces an LLM that is competitive with top proprietary models!

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Can generative models create their own training data? Recent research indicates that we should be careful with doing this! For image generation models especially, there seems to be a reasonable risk of degradation (or even a complete collapse) in performance…
What is self-consumption? Self-consumption (also called autophagy) in the context of generative AI describes the process of using a model to generate its own training data. There are many setups for this that include different ratios of real/synthetic data. The impact of self-consumption is not fully understood. It is useful for image classification, but what about image generation? This question is incredibly important, as datasets used to train popular models like Stable Diffusion are known to contain synthetic data!
Fully-synthetic = bad. Recent research shows that fully-synthetic loops (i.e., continually training a model only with data that it generates) yields a clear performance degradation in image generation models. Both the quality and diversity of models’ generations decrease significantly.
Adding synthetic data to a fixed dataset = ok. When we take a fixed, real dataset and slowly augment the data with synthetic generations from our model, the generative model will still experience performance degradation! But, this process happens a bit more slowly compared to a fully-synthetic loop. [5/9]
Mixing synthetic + real data = good. However, when we are constantly mixing synthetically-generated data with new, real data, performance degradations can be avoided! Thus, the key to self-consumption is to constantly augment synthetic training data with fresh data taken from the real world.
Don’t use too much synthetic data! The key here is that we need to be careful about how much synthetic data that we include! Too much synthetic data can still lead to performance issues. There seems to be a threshold that dictates the maximum “admissible” amount of synthetic data used for training.

summary:
Open-source LLMs are now commonly used and widely studied, but this area of research saw some initial struggles and criticism due to the poor performance of models like OPT and BLOOM. These four recently-proposed open-source models changed this narrative…
LLaMA. Interest in open-source LLM research skyrocketed with the proposal of LLaMA, a suite of several LLMs with sizes between 7 billion and 65 billion parameters. These models were the first high-performing open-source base LLMs, though they could only be used for research.
MPT. LLaMA was quickly followed by the release of MPT-7B and MPT-30B. In addition to being commercially-usable, MPT models perform well. MPT-7B is comparable to LLaMA-7B, while MPT-30B performs similarly to GPT-3. Interestingly, MPT models are known to be especially strong on coding benchmarks.
Falcon. The release of the Falcon suite of LLMs, including Falcon-7B and Falcon-40B, was met with a lot of excitement. These models set the new state-of-the-art for open-source LLMs. Pre-trained on a massive custom-curated corpus, Falcon models perform incredibly well and were unmatched in their quality until very recently.
LLaMA-2. Similar to its predecessor, LLaMA-2 is trained on a massive corpus of public data. However, the pre-training dataset used for LLaMA-2 is 40% larger and uses a different mix, leading to significantly improved performance. Plus, the models are available under a (somewhat restrictive) commercial license and use an architecture that is optimized for faster inference.
What made these models so much better? They pre-train over a lot more data! OPT and BLOOM are trained on 180 billion and 341 billion tokens, respectively. The datasets used to pre-train the models above have the following sizes:
- LLaMA: 1.4 trillion tokens
- MPT: 1 trillion token
- Falcon: 1-1.5 trillion token
- LLaMA-2: 2 trillion tokens

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
There’s been a lot of recent discussion about the Gorilla language model. This unique model learns the ability to coordinate, access, and use a variety of different deep learning model APIs as tools for problem solving. Here’s how the LLM is trained to do this...
Tool usage in LLMs. Recently, research on language models has heavily explored the idea of integrating LLMs with external tools, either via a prompting (e.g., HuggingGPT) or fine-tuning approach (e.g., Toolformer). LLMs can learn to use a variety of tools (e.g., search engines, calculators, etc.) by just learning to generate a call to an API associated with the tool.
Deep Learning Models as Tools. One of the most interesting types of tools that an LLM can learn to use is other deep learning models. Countless models exist for solving specific, useful tasks (e.g., object detectors, classifiers, image generators, etc.) and can oftentimes be queried for their output using online APIs.
Gorilla. The Gorilla LLM uses a fine-tuning approach to learn how to leverage a massive set of external deep learning model APIs when solving problems. Using the self-instruct framework, authors generate a dataset of valid API calls to over 1,600 different deep learning models (from HuggingFace, PyTorch Hub, and TensorFlow Hub) that are used to fine-tune the LLM.
Models as tools. The deep learning models that Gorilla learns how to use span a variety of domains, including CV, audio, RL, and more. The relevant information and documentation for each deep learning model API is stored as a json object. GPT-4 generates ten user question prompts and associated responses to go with each API, which are then filtered based on correctness.
Retrieval-aware fine-tuning. The fine-tuning process used by Gorilla is a bit different than typical SFT. The model uses retrieval-aware fine-tuning to learn how to make valid API calls. This might sound complex, but really it just means that, in the fine-tuning dataset, we prepend every call to an API with up-to-date documentation for that API.
“Supporting a web scale collection of potentially millions of changing APIs requires rethinking our approach to how we integrate tools.” - from Gorilla paper
Why is Gorilla unique? Because of its retrieval-aware fine-tuning approach, the Gorilla model learns to leverage an API's current documentation to craft valid API calls. As such, the model can adopt a retrieval approach at test time that retrieves up-to-date documentation, allowing the model to properly leverage thousands of tools with (potentially) changing documentation when attempt to solve a problem.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Have you ever wondered why all language models use decoder-only architectures? It's partially because decoder-only models work great for next-token prediction. However, recent research has also analyzed the choice of architecture for language models in depth...
Decoder-only architecture. Transformers have two “stacks” of layers by default: the encoder and the decoder. A decoder-only transformer discards the encoder, leaving only a decoder with several layers of alternating masked self-attention and feed-forward transformations.
Perfect for next token prediction. The decoder-only architecture works well for next token prediction due to its use of masked self-attention. We can process a sequence of tokens, then train the model to predict the next token at every position in the sequence. Each token’s output representation only depends on the tokens that come before it.
What about other architectures? If we perform next token prediction with an encoder-decoder or encoder-only architecture, we must ingest a prefix and predict the next token. Due to the use of bidirectional self-attention, next token prediction can’t be applied to intermediate tokens in the sequence.
"All state-of-the-art language models over 100 billion parameters are causal decoder-only models. This is in opposition to the findings of [T5], in which encoder-decoder models significantly outperform decoder-only models for transfer learning." - from BLOOM paper
Analysis from T5. The T5 model analyzed a variety of different transformer architectures and training paradigms, finding that the encoder-decoder transformer (with a Cloze pre-training objective) works best for transfer learning setups (i.e., pre-training, then fine-tuning on a certain task). But, does this apply to language modeling?
Analysis from BLOOM. Interestingly, the BLOOM publication performs a similar analysis for language model pre-training, where a variety of different transformer architectures are pre-trained using a language modeling objective. As expected, we see that decoder-only models perform best after pre-training in this regime, explaining why this architecture is so popular for LLMs.
“We evaluated encoder-decoder and decoder-only architectures and their interactions with causal, prefix, and masked language modeling pretraining objectives. Our results show that immediately after pre-training, causal decoder-only models performed best - validating the choice of state-of-the-art LLMs.” - from BLOOM paper
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F2twEMcW0AAezjO.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
I just finished writing a survey on the history of open-source LLM research, spanning from the early days (e.g., OPT and BLOOM) to recent models like LLaMA-2. Here are three takeaways that seem to have the biggest impact on LLM quality…
Base models make all the difference. Pre-training is the first, most expensive, and most important step of training an LLM. If your base model is bad, then you can’t fix it with extensive fine-tuning. We learn from open-source LLM research (LIMA) that most of the LLM's knowledge base is gained during pre-training, while fine-tuning/alignment serves to learn the correct style/format.
Going further, major surges in open-source LLM research seem to be catalyzed by the release of powerful base models (e.g., LLaMA led to a wave of research on imitation learning). Plus, we see in a variety of papers that improving the underlying base model yields improvements after fine-tuning and alignment. Creating a good base model is difficult, but it makes all the difference!
Data is important. When we compare early attempts at open-source LLMs (e.g., OPT or BLOOM) to recent models like LLaMA-2, the largest difference between them is the data! LLaMA-2 is pre-trained over 2 trillion tokens of high-quality data, while OPT/BLOOM observe ~500M tokens of data during pre-training combined!
Additionally, we learn from LIMA and LLaMA-2 that, during both pre-training and alignment, the quality of data matters. Increasing the amount of data used for SFT has minimal impact, but ensuring the diversity and quality of this data (even if there are very few examples) massively benefits performance. Data quality and quantity matters across all steps of LLM training.
Alignment goes a long way. We see with LLaMA-2 that one of the largest remaining gaps between open-source and proprietary LLMs is the quality of alignment. Most open-source LLMs are fine-tuning using solely SFT over public sources of data that oftentimes lack in quality and diversity. On the other hand, closed-source models are aligned with SFT and RLHF over large proprietary datasets.
“Llama 2-Chat is the result of several months of research and iterative applications of alignment techniques, including both instruction tuning and RLHF, requiring significant computational and annotation resources.” - from LLaMA-2 paper
To close this gap, LLaMA-2-Chat models undergo an extensive alignment process, including multiple phases of SFT and RLHF. In total, 100K dialogue examples are used for SFT, as well as 1M instances of human feedback for RLHF. The resulting model is, by far, the highest-performing open-source LLM to yet be created, thus revealing the pivotal importance of fine-tuning and alignment.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Using a KV cache is one of the most commonly-used tricks for speeding up inference with LLMs. Here’s exactly how it works…
Autoregressive decoding process. When we perform inference with an LLM, it follows an autoregressive decoding process. Put simply, this means that we i) start with a sequence of textual tokens, ii) predict the next token, iii) add this token to our input, and iv) repeat until generation is finished.
Causal self-attention. Self-attention within a language model is causal, meaning that each token only considers itself and prior tokens when computing its representation (i.e., NOT future tokens). As such, representations for each token do not change during autoregressive decoding! We need to compute the representation for each new token, but other tokens remain fixed (i.e., because they don’t depend on tokens that follow them).
Caching self-attention values. When we perform self-attention, we project our sequence of tokens using three separate, linear projections: key projection, value projection, and query projection. Then, we executed self-attention using the resulting matrices! The KV-cache simply stores the results of the key and value projections for future decoding iterations so that we don’t recompute them every time!
Why not cache the query? We might immediately be wondering why the key and value projections are cached, but not the query. This is simply because the rest of the entries in the query matrix are only needed to compute the representations of prior tokens in the sequence. For computing the representation of the most recently added token, we only need access to the most recent row in the query matrix.
Updates to the KV cache. Throughout autoregressive decoding, we have the key and value projections cached. Each time we get a new token in our input, we simply compute the new rows as part of self-attention and add them to the KV cache. Then, we can use the query projection for the new token and the updated key and value projections to perform the rest of the forward pass.
Important note. Here, we have considered single-headed self-attention for simplicity. However, it’s important to note that the same exact process applies to the multi-headed self-attention used by LLMs. We just perform the exact same process in parallel across multiple attention heads.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
I have recently given some long-form lectures on language models, how they work, and the AI landscape, which has given me a chance to more clearly organize key concepts for understanding language models. Here are the 15 key concepts that I’ve arrived at so far…
AI Basics/History: LLMs aren’t everything, and there is a lot of AI research surrounding them.
1. (Self-)supervised learning techniques have a common framework, including a task, a model, some data, and a training algorithm.
2. AI has a long history (dating back to the early 20th century) of leveraging this framework to solve important problems.
3. Deep learning (and language models, which are a small subset of deep learning) is an area of AI that has become especially successful due to the ability to leverage large-scale data/compute.
Language Model Fundamentals: How do we create a good base model?
4. The transformer architecture (and self-attention) is a fundamental advancement that empowered the recent explosion of language models.
5. Using decoder-only transformers and next-token prediction, we can pre-train language models to gain a vast amount of knowledge and linguistic understanding.
6. After pre-training, we have a foundation model that can be used to solve various tasks via in-context learning.
7. To make these foundation models as good as possible, we need both large models (many parameters) and as much data as possible (i.e., large models alone are not enough).
Modern Language Models: How do we go from a good base model to something like ChatGPT?
8. Next-token prediction is not enough to create something like ChatGPT. Base Model output can be repetitive and uninteresting. We need to align the model to human desires/expectations.
9. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) performs alignment by fine-tuning the model (using next-token prediction) on examples of good responses to prompts.
10. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) aligns the language model directly based on human feedback to its responses.
11. The best/top language models today are extensively aligned via a combination of SFT and RLHF.
Applying Language Models: How to we apply language models to solving specific problems?
12. Fine-tuning language models (using next-token prediction) on in-domain data is a great way to specialize these models for a specific application domain.
13. In-domain fine-tuning is not always necessary because there is a lot we can accomplish via in-context learning!
14. Especially when the underlying model is steerable, a lot can be done with more basic prompting techniques, such as zero/few-shot and instruction prompting.
15. We should only use advanced prompting approaches after empirically confirming that we cannot solve a problem with simpler techniques. Start simple, perform tests, and add complexity only as needed.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The recent success of LLaMA-2, which can be attributed to a variety of factors, clearly demonstrates the massive value of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). Here’s what the authors of LLaMA have to say about why RLHF is so important…
Collecting data for RLHF. LLaMA-2’s data collection process for RLHF follows a binary protocol. Human annotators first write a prompt according to some alignment property like helpfulness or safety. Then, the model is used to generate two responses and the annotator labels the preferred response.
Training a reward model. Using this human preference data, we can train a reward model. The reward model shares the same architecture and weights as the language model but has an added regression head and is fine-tuned (using a ranking loss) to predict human preference when given a prompt and response pair as input.
Fine-tuning with reinforcement learning. Once a reward model is created, it can be used to automate/predict human feedback for fine-tuning. We can optimize the LLM to maximize human preference with reinforcement learning algorithms like PPO or rejection sampling fine-tuning. LLaMA-2 uses both of these approaches in sequence during alignment.
Open-source models emphasize SFT. Typically, aligning a language model is done via a combination of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). However, most open-source models seem to focus upon SFT and fail to rely extensively on RLHF. The authors of LLaMA-2 originally planned to take a similar approach!
“Many among us expressed a preference for supervised annotation, attracted by its denser signal… However, reinforcement learning proved highly effective, particularly given its cost and time effectiveness. Our findings underscore that the crucial determinant of RLHF’s success lies in the synergy it fosters between humans and LLMs throughout the annotation process.” - from LLaMA-2 paper
RLHF is important. Instead of avoiding RLHF, authors of LLaMA-2 learned to embrace and emphasize this approach during the process of creating LLaMA-2, as it fosters a “synergy” between humans and LLMs during alignment. In particular, there are a few specific reasons (outlined below) RLHF is found to be so useful.
Writing responses is noisy. Human annotators must write responses to generate data for SFT, which is a noisy process! The variance in human writing abilities is high, meaning that some responses are likely to be of low quality. Unavoidably, the model must learn from such poor examples (at least in part) during SFT.
Preference annotations are easy. While manually writing responses for SFT can be difficult, RLHF only requires that humans provide binary preference feedback to the LLM, which is less noisy and easier to accomplish. Interestingly, humans can even provide reliable preference labels for responses that go beyond their own writing ability. High-quality responses are easy to identify but hard to write from scratch.
Going beyond human abilities. Responses are generated by the LLM during RLHF. Authors of LLaMA-2 note that such responses can surpass the writing abilities of human annotators, which is not possible when humans are used to annotate data for SFT.
TL;DR. RLHF is incredibly powerful, and it is not a coincidence that LLaMA-2 models perform so well given their emphasis upon both SFT and RLHF. We see in the analysis of LLaMA-2 that using RLHF slowly suppresses low-quality outputs from the model over time and drastically improves the model’s behavior with respect to desired alignment criteria (i.e., helpfulness and safety).
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F3hOUiwWIAAPlt2.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
DeciCoder-1B is a commercially open-source (Apache 2.0) code LLM that was just released. The model is inference efficient and performs well. The write-up for the model mentions some interesting (non-standard) ideas that seem like they could be really impactful…
The dataset. DeciCoder is trained on the Stack dataset, which has 6TB of code from >350 programming languages. But, the dataset is filtered to only include Python, Java, and Javascript code. So, DeciCoder is an open-source code-completion model for these three languages.
Training objective. DeciCoder doesn’t use a language modeling objective for training. Rather, a fill-in-the-middle (FIM) approach is used (i.e., aims to complete missing or broken pieces of text), as described in “Efficient Training of Language Models to Fill in the Middle”. The authors of FIM extensively evaluate on code (and HumanEval in particular), finding that FIM is more efficient and yields similar performance compared to a standard language modeling objective.
Neural architecture search. Typical neural architecture search (NAS) algorithms are too slow/heavy to use with LLMs. But, DeciCoder uses an efficient algorithm called AutoNAC to optimize its architecture for efficiency based on the particular GPU being used for inference (i.e., NVIDIA A10). The result is a model that uses grouped query attention (similar to LLaMA-2) with more attention heads and fewer layers compared to comparable open-source code models.
LLM architecture hyperparameters. DeciCoder’s use of a shallower architecture with more attention heads per layer is interesting. Several works on transformers (e.g., see “Multi-head or Single-head? An Empirical Comparison for Transformer Training” and “Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?”) indicate that a single self-attention head (potentially with more layers) works well. Here, we see that a shallower model with more attention heads can perform well and achieve impressive throughput.
Performance. DeciCoder, which has a 2K context length, is evaluated largely on the HumanEval dataset (originally proposed by the Codex language model). The model is provided a function signature and a docstring as input and evaluated based on its ability to output a function. DeciCoder outperforms comparable open-source models like SantaCoder on HumanEval.
TL;DR. DeciCoder isn’t instruction tuned, so there is more that can be done with it. But, the writeup provides a lot of impactful ideas. Exploring efficient (hardware-aware) variants of NAS for LLMs is pretty interesting, especially given the need for inference efficiency when hosting open-source LLMs. Plus, seeing successful applications of language modeling alternatives (e.g., FIM) is interesting. DeciCoder is both an interesting read and a useful starting point for open-source code applications with language models.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Have you ever played with the topP parameter on chat/text completion APIs? This parameter, based upon a technique called nucleus sampling, is a great way to control the randomness of a language model’s output. Here’s how it works…
Autoregressive decoding. When we generate a textual sequence with a language model, we typically begin with a textual prefix/prompt. Then, we follow the steps shown below:
1. Use the language model to generate the next token
2. Add this output token to our input sequence
3. Repeat
By continually generating the next token in this manner (i.e., this is what we call the autoregressive decoding process), we can generate an entire textual sequence. But, how do we choose/predict the next token (i.e., step one shown above)?
Token probabilities. Instead of directly outputting the next token, language models output a probability distribution over the set of all possible tokens. Given this probability distribution, we can follow several different strategies for selecting the next token. For example, greedy decoding (one potential strategy) just selects the token with the highest probability as the next token!
Temperature setting. We can leverage the temperature setting to “tweak” the probability distribution over tokens. Temperature is simply a hyperparameter in the softmax transformation (see image for equations) used to generate the token probability distribution. Higher temperature values result in a more uniform distribution over tokens, while lower values create a distribution that assigns high probability to a single token.
Nucleus sampling, which has a hyperparameter topP, chooses from the smallest possible set of tokens whose summed probability exceeds topP during decoding. Given this set of tokens, we re-normalize the probability distribution based on each token’s respective probability and then sample! This is different from topK, which just samples from the K tokens with the highest probability.
Why is nucleus sampling useful? Consider a case where a single token has a very high probability (i.e., larger than topP). In this case, nucleus sampling will always sample this token. Alternatively, assigning more uniform probability across tokens may cause a larger number of tokens to be considered during decoding. Put simply, nucleus sampling can dynamically adjust the number of tokens that are considered during decoding based on their probabilities.
Practical usage. Nucleus sampling can be controlled by setting the topP parameter in most language model APIs. Notably, we should only use either nucleus sampling or temperature, as APIs such as OpenAI say that these parameters cannot be used in tandem. Put simply, these are different and disjoint methods of controlling the randomness of a language model’s output.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Advanced prompting techniques allow language models to solve complex problems but are often constrained to a single line of reasoning. Tree of thoughts (ToT) prompting avoids this by deliberately decomposing, planning, and exploring candidate solutions to a problem via a four-part framework…
Prior prompting techniques. Powerful prompting techniques (e.g., chain of thought prompting and self-consistency) have been developed for solving complex, reasoning-based problems with LLMs. However, these approaches solve problems using next token prediction, where a solution is outputted left-to-right in a single attempt! This falls short for difficult problems that require exploration, backtracking, and lookahead.
“A genuine problem-solving process involves the repeated use of available information to initiate exploration, which discloses, in turn, more information until a way to attain the solution is finally discovered.” - from Report on a general problem solving program (published in late 1950s!)
Inspiration from prior work. In the mid 20th century, AI researchers proposed that solving a problem can be formulated as search through a combinatorial solution space represented as a tree. Each node in this tree is a partial solution and connections between nodes are operators that increment/update a partial solution. ToT prompting formalizes this idea in the prompt engineering context to solve complex problems with LLMs.
Implementing ToT prompting is different depending on the task we are trying to solve. But, any instantiation of this idea must define four standard components:
1. Thought decomposition: We must decide what defines an intermediate solution (or thought) for our problem and how a solution can be decomposed into individual thoughts.
2. Thought generation: We must determine how to generate potential thoughts. This is done by prompting an LLM either independently or sequentially (depending upon whether duplicate thoughts are likely).
3. State evaluation: We must define how intermediate states (i.e., partial solutions to a problem) will be evaluated. Again, this is usually done by prompting a language model to score an intermediate solution or compare it to another intermediate solution.
4. Search for a solution: Finally, we must select a search algorithm that will be used to explore intermediate solutions and find a final solution. We can use common algorithms like breadth-first or depth-first search.
Example implementation. Consider a problem that takes four random numbers as inputs and outputs an arithmetic operation that equals 24 and uses each of these numbers once. ToT prompting decomposes a solution to this problem into three thoughts, each of which is an intermediate equation. We evaluate and generate states by prompting an LLM to either generate the next operation or evaluate whether reaching the number 24 is possible from the current equation. Then, we find a solution with breadth-first search.
TL;DR: ToT prompting is an approach that allows complex, multi-step problems to be solved with LLMs. By decomposing solutions to a problem into individual steps or thoughts, ToT prompting enables sophisticated exploration of the solution space via multiple lines of reasoning with support for strategic lookahead, backtracking, and more. Then, we can search for solutions to problems within this framework via a combination of prompting and self-evaluation with well-known search algorithms for graph-structured data.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Training on English-only data is becoming a standard for language models. I’ve recently started to wonder: What are we missing by not considering other languages? A few quick thoughts on why exploring multilingual language models would be beneficial…
TL;DR. Most language models only train on English data. If we consider other languages, it could give us access to more data and extra beneficial information. Training multilingual models does come with difficulties from a technical perspective, but I hope that English-only language models don't become a long-term standard. Building multilingual support makes this powerful technology more beneficial for everyone.
Language filtering. Recently, most data used for pre-training language models (especially open-source models; e.g., Falcon, LLaMA, and OLMo) is English-only. When data is scraped from the web, the first filtering operation applied to the data is a language filter. We use a FastText classifier to identify the language, then simply remove anything that is not English.
Data scale. We have seen within recent research on language models (Chinchilla, Falcon, LLaMa-2, etc.) that pre-training the base model over more data yields a massive benefit. Although we can construct massive corpora of English-only data, the scale of accessible data increases massively as we consider data in other languages. This larger scale of data could yield a massive benefit if leveraged properly.
Cultural context. Beyond having access to more data, there is a lot of relevant cultural information that may be missing within English-only text. By training on languages other than English, we could significantly increase the model’s knowledge base with this extra important information. Put simply, there is useful information in the world that goes beyond what has been written in English.
Inclusiveness in applications. Finally, language models should not only be accessible to those that speak English. Given the incredible potential of this technology, it makes sense to build support for many languages (especially in the open-source domain) so that more people can use and build with these models.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
One of the best ways to reduce hallucinations with LLMs is by retrieving useful, factual information and injecting it into the LLM’s prompt as added context. Although this might sound complicated, it’s actually quite easy to implement with standard vector search functionality…
Why do we need this? All LLMs have a fixed context length. So, the amount of information we can include in a prompt is limited by nature! As such, we need to be selective about the context that we provide to our model. If we want to provide useful context that can reduce hallucinations and improve the model’s output, one of the best approaches is to retrieve relevant information from an external (vector) database.
Retrieval framework for LLMs. Assuming that we have a lot of relevant textual data that can be used by an LLM, we can’t just inject all of this data into the model’s prompt every time that we perform inference. Rather, we need to do the following:
1. Break our data into textual chunks
2. Vectorize each of the textual chunks
3. Store these vectors (with their data) in a vector database
4. Find relevant data at inference time using vector search
5. Add relevant data to our prompt to provide more context to the LLM
We will use the same embedding model to vectorize these chunks and to generate query vectors that can be used for search.
Storing data in a vector db. The first step in the above framework is to chunk our data. Typically, we will use chunks of ~200 tokens. However, the optimal chunk size is a hyperparameter that can change depending on the application. Then, we use an embedding model to vectorize each of these chunks, and we can store them, along with their text data, in a vector database (e.g., Redis, Weaviate, Pinecone, Qdrant, etc.).
Retrieving relevant context. When we want to retrieve relevant textual data from our vector db, we should just i) create a query embedding based on our prompt (possibly including the chat history) and ii) run a vector search for relevant documents. This way, we can use semantic search to identify portions of data that are relevant to include as context within the LLM’s prompt.
Creating the query embedding. There are a ton of different ways we can create query embedding for searching our vector db. The simplest approach would be to truncate our chat history or prompt and pass this directly into the embedding model. But, if this is too long, we could ask the LLM to summarize our chat history or prompt before embedding it, or even to convert the chat history or prompt into a list of search keywords.
Picking an embedding model. To make sure this works well, we need a good embedding model that captures the semantic similarities between our queries and textual chunks. There are a variety of good embedding models publicly available via SentenceTransformers and HuggingFace. To find one that works for you, I’d recommend taking a look at the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (hosted on HuggingFace).
The result. We can use the approach described above to power retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which is one of the best ways to reduce hallucinations and improve the output of LLMs. Given that this approach can be implemented without significant effort via tools like Pinecone / Weaviate and HuggingFace / SentenceTransformers, it is undoubtedly one of the most useful practical tools for building with LLMs.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Research on advanced prompting techniques for language models has extended chain of thought and tree of thought prompting to graph-structured reasoning processes. But, did you know that there are two versions of “graph of thought” prompting that have been proposed already?
Some background. Advanced prompting techniques like chain of thought and tree of thought prompting have drastically improved the ability of large language models to solve complex, reasoning-based tasks. Forcing the LLM to construct a step-by-step response to a problem drastically improves its problem-solving capabilities, but all of these techniques assume that the reasoning process is linear.
“Human thinking is often characterized by its ability to make sudden leaps and connections between seemingly unrelated ideas, which can lead to novel insights and solutions. This non-linear, jumping thought process is a hallmark of human creativity, reasoning, and problem-solving abilities.” - from [1]
Graph-based reasoning. Humans do not seem to perform reasoning based on individual chains of thought. Rather, we make leaps and connections between ideas that lead to novel insights. Inspired by this idea, researchers have recently extended chain and tree of thoughts prompting to a graph-structured approach. We will take a look here at two (independent) papers that have already been written on this topic.
Graph of thought reasoning (GOTR). In [1], authors proposed a two-stage technique that:
1. Outputs a problem solving rationale given text (and potentially images) as input.
2. Outputs a final answer given the original input concatenated with a rationale.
This approach uses an encoder-decoder structure and is fine-tuned end-to-end. Several encoders ingest data from each of the different modalities that are considered. The output of these encoders is combined in a fusion layer, then passed to a decoder to generate output.
Where does the graph come in? So far, it seems like GOTR does not use any graphs within its reasoning process. However, the model creates a named entity graph based on the input text and generated rationale. Then, this graph is ingested by a graph attention network encoder and combined with all image/text features. As such, the decoder receives information from text, image, and graph-based inputs!
GoT prompting. In [2], authors follow a more traditional prompting approach, called graph of thought (GoT) prompting, that uses a system of causal LLMs and prompts to perform reasoning according to a graph structure. The reasoning process is modeled as a graph, where each node represents a thought or (partial) solution and connections indicate that a certain thought was generated from some other thought.
A system of LLMs. GoT prompting has several “modules” that control the reasoning process, including a top-level controller (controls the reasoning process), a parser (verifies and extracts LLM output), a scorer (judges the quality of solutions), and a prompter (writes prompts for each different module). Together, these modules can transform the underlying graph structure and work towards solving a reasoning problem.
TL;DR: Modeling an LLM’s reasoning process as a graph structure can be beneficial for certain problems and is (arguably) more comparable to the human reasoning process. But, these techniques tend to be more costly than basic CoT prompting and only provide a tangible benefit on select problems. For more details, check out the overview of these techniques that I just wrote for my newsletter.
--------
[1] Yao, Yao, Zuchao Li, and Hai Zhao. "Beyond Chain-of-Thought, Effective Graph-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models." arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.16582 (2023).
[2] Besta, Maciej, et al. "Graph of Thoughts: Solving Elaborate Problems with Large Language Models." arXiv preprint arXiv:2308.09687 (2023).

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The OLMo language model (from AI2) is currently under development. It seems like this model, when released, will be a massive contribution to open-source LLM research. Here’s the four main reasons I’m excited about OLMo…
(1) Step forward in transparency. OLMo is being heavily documented to provide researchers with better insight into the LLM training process (e.g., logbooks, code, etc.) Such an approach is quite similar to the Open Pre-trained Transformers (OPT) library from Meta that was released at the beginning of the open-source LLM revolution, but recent open-source LLMs have not typically included such detailed logbooks of the training process in their releases. In my opinion, such resources are invaluable for researchers looking to replicate the creation of such models!
(2) Code mixing. The creators of OLMo indicate that including a mix of code in the pre-training process can improve overall reasoning performance and heavily benefit the resulting model. Recent open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-2, though this was amended partially with the release of code LLaMA) have been criticized for poor coding abilities. But, authors claim that OLMo will be trained over a sufficient mix of code, comparable to MPT or Gopher. Plus, a specialized processing pipeline is adopted for code data to ensure high-quality code is used for pre-training.
(3) More data. Speaking of pre-training data, OLMo is being trained over a new dataset called DoLMA that contains over 3T tokens. This dataset is significantly bigger than pre-training corpora used by other models (e.g., LLaMA-2 pre-trained over 2T tokens, Falcon-40B over 1T tokens, etc.). The DoLMA dataset has already been released (under a custom ImppACT license written by AI2), so researchers can even start working with this data now! Similar to RefinedWeb, I think this dataset will become a beneficial resource that makes language model pre-training more accessible.
(4) Data filtering and construction. Similar to trend being followed by Falcon and LLaMA-2 in creating pre-training datasets, DoLMA is constructed via a set of simple filtering heuristics, rather than by using ML-based filtering rules that may produce downstream bias. Although the model is still English-only, the creation of DoLMA will be extensively documented (useful for those who want to create their own pre-training corpus) and emphasize quality and diversity.
TL;DR. OLMo is a new open-source language model being released by AI2. This model will be valuable because i) a lot of resources and documentations will be included with it and ii) the model is pre-trained over a new and impressive dataset called DoLMA. The quality and mix of data (for pre-training or fine-tuning!) makes all the difference for creating state-of-the-art language models.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Powerful LLMs like GPT-4 can follow complex instructions, but building applications with less capable LLMs requires breaking a single, detailed instruction into a “chain” of simpler prompts. Here’s an overview of practically useful chaining techniques for LLMs...
Some background. Typically, we interact with an LLM by passing the model some textual input (a prompt) and receiving textual output. Prompt chains are not much different from this! We still leverage the text-to-text structure of the LLM, but we prompt the model several times in sequence. Additionally, the exact sequence of prompts that we use might be dynamically adapted based on the language model’s output.
Sequential chain. The first type of chain that is useful is just a sequential chain! Here, we just have a pre-defined sequence of prompts that we want to pass to the LLM. This sequence of prompts does not change depending on the model’s output, but we can pass the output of the LLM after each prompt as part of the input for the next prompting step.
Router chain. What if we don’t want to always use the same sequence of prompts? In this case, we can use a router chain, which gives the LLM multiple options for the prompt to use next and lets the model choose. Typically, this is done by providing the LLM descriptions of each of the prompts that are available, then prompting the model to generate an output that indicates which of these prompts should be called.
Different router chain options. Sometimes, asking the LLM to choose the next prompt that it should use can be difficult, especially if we are using a less capable LLM and have several different prompt options available. In these cases, there are a few different types of router chains we can use that reduce the cognitive load (or difficulty) of the LLM’s task:
1. Embedding router: Instead of asking the LLM to choose the next prompt, generate an embedding for the current prompt and all prompt options in the router chain and select the next prompt based on cosine similarity.
2. Sequential router: We can break the router decision into multiple, smaller steps (i.e., just form a sequential router chain!). In most cases, it is easiest to make each “step” in the sequential router chain a simple yes/no decision for the model (e.g., is this a science question? Is this a math question? etc.)
TL;DR: Prompt chains are a huge part of successfully using LLMs in practice! If you can get a good sense for how to break a difficult problem into multiple, smaller steps that can each be solved with a prompt, you can probably build a variety of impressive AI applications. Put simply, prompt chains allow us to break difficult problems into sequences of smaller (dynamically-chosen) steps that the LLM can more reliably solve.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F49cKC8WsAAXC8U.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Next token prediction is the workhorse of causal language models. Despite recent advancements, LLMs' capabilities are largely attributable to next token prediction. To better grasp this concept, let’s study an implementation of next token prediction for LLM pretaining...
Background: Next token prediction is the most commonly-used pretraining objective for causal language models. It takes a sequence of text as input and trains the underlying model to predict the next token for every token within this sequence. Because the ground truth next token is already present within the underlying text (i.e., the “labels” are implicit), this is a self-supervised training objective. We can construct a dataset for next token prediction pretraining by just downloading a massive corpus of text data from the internet.
Constructing input and using our model: During pretraining, our LLM takes a sequence (or multiple sequences in the case of a mini-batch) as input. We can pass this raw text through a tokenizer to break each sequence into discrete tokens. Then, we embed these tokens (including positional embeddings) and pass the resulting sequence of vectors into a decoder-only transformer, which produces output vectors for each token via a sequence of several feed-forward and causal self-attention layers.
Predicting the next token: For each token within every sequence of our mini-batch, the decoder-only transformer outputs a vector. We perform next token prediction not just over the last token in each sequence, but in parallel across every token within every sequence. This is possible due to the use of causal self-attention in the transformer. No token has knowledge of those that come after it. To predict the next token, we use a linear layer to project a token’s output vector into a probability distribution over the token vocabulary. This is just a vector with the same size as our vocabulary, and we apply softmax to make it a distribution.
Applying the loss: To apply the next token prediction loss, we just use a cross entropy loss across all predicted next tokens. This loss encourages the model to maximize the probability of the ground truth next token over all tokens within every sequence of our input. Notably, this is the same loss that we would use for any normal classification task! We are just teaching the model to correctly classify the next token within every position of every sequence.
The implementation: To implement this training objective, we don’t have to do much! We just need to create a PyTorch model for our decoder-only transformer, write a data loader to obtain pretraining data, and create a training loop that can apply the next token prediction loss. In the attached image, we examine a simple implementation provided within NanoGPT by Andrej Karpathy. Here, we can see that the code exactly matches the discussion of language model pretraining provided above. The only changes required are related to distributed training and automatic mixed precision (AMP) training, which are used to make LLM training more efficient/fast.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
What is the legality of training deep learning models on the output of proprietary LLMs? Initially, I thought this would be completely prohibited for industrial use cases, but I'm wondering if there are exceptions...
What we know: The terms and conditions of proprietary LLMs like GPT-4 (and others) clearly state that you can't use the output of the model to train a "competing" model. As such, LLMs trained via an imitation approach (e.g., Alpaca or Vicuna), because they clearly use the output of a proprietary LLM to create an open-source replica, can only be used for research. But, the definition of "competing" is unclear. What applications does this actually restrict?
Let's consider a few common use cases in industry and analyze whether these applications are prohibited from training on the output of a proprietary model.
[Use Case 1] LLMs for internal use: Many companies are interested in creating private language models that i) are trained over internal/specialized data and ii) can be used by employees to automate their work (e.g., customer support or coding assistants). If these models are only used internally to boost productivity, is this considered commercial use? Is this competitive with proprietary LLMs? It is unclear to me whether training on outputs from GPT-4, which could heavily benefit performance, would be legal for such an application
[Background] Fine-tuning RAG: One of the best ways to improve the performance of an LLM-based system is via retrieval augmented generation (RAG). Especially when we cannot fine-tune the underlying LLM (e.g., maybe we are using an API), RAG allows us to retrieve and inject useful, up-to-date information into the model's context. RAG relies upon an embedding model to retrieve relevant data and (optionally) a cross-encoder (or other re-ranking model) to rank the results.
[Use Case 2] RAG with chat sessions: Assume we are performing RAG, but the data being retrieved are chat sessions from GPT-4. Additionally, assume that we are working on a commercial chat system that is perceived as competitive with GPT-4. In this case, can we fine-tune the embedding and re-ranking models used for RAG? The data used to fine-tuning these models are chat sessions that contain output from GPT-4, and the overall system is competitive. However, the individual models are not necessarily competitive with any LLM.
TL;DR: The terms and conditions for proprietary LLMs prevent us from using their output to train competing models, but the scope of this restriction is somewhat unclear. Does a model compete if it is only used internally at a company? What about other deep learning models that are not LLMs? The legal landscape of AI is highly dynamic, so it will be very interesting to see how these questions get answered over time.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Adversarial prompting aims to craft a prompt for an LLM that elicits unexpected, harmful or negative behavior. Adversarial prompts are worrisome for anyone building LLM-based applications, but recent research is developing accurate methods of detecting these attacks!
Paper Title: CERTIFYING LLM SAFETY AGAINST ADVERSARIAL PROMPTING
Main Idea: This paper introduces an “erase-and-check” framework that can defend against adversarial prompts. Within the input prompt, tokens are individually erased/removed, and the resulting subsequences are inspected using a safety filter. If any subsequences are detected as harmful by the filter, then the entire input prompt is considered harmful. Such an approach is effective because it causes any adversarial modification to a normal prompt (e.g., a suffix, internal sequence, several tokens inserted at strategic positions, etc.) to be flagged as harmful.
Empirical Results: “Empirical results demonstrate that our technique obtains strong certified safety guarantees on harmful prompts while maintaining good performance on safe prompts. For example, against adversarial suffixes of length 20, it certifiably detects 93% of the harmful prompts and labels 94% of the safe prompts as safe using the open source language model Llama 2 as the safety filter.”

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Almost all generative language models use a decoder-only transformer architecture, making the decoder-only transformer one of the most influential architectures in modern AI. Let’s take a deeper look at an implementation to understand exactly how it works…
Implementation credits: The implementation of a decoder-only transformer we will examine in this post is taken from the NanoGPT repository, created by Andrej Karpathy. This repository implements pretraining of a (large) language model—GPT-2 in particular—in only ~600 lines of code. It is an awesome learning resource.
Block definition: Each block of the decoder-only transformer contains causal self-attention and a feed-forward transformation. Given an input, we apply layer normalization and causal self-attention, followed by a residual connection. Then, we apply layer normalization again, followed by a feed-forward layer and another residual connection. The decoder-only architecture has several blocks; e.g., GPT/GPT-2 has 12 total blocks.
Embedding layers: The decoder-only model has two different embedding layers that it defines. The first embedding layer stores token embeddings for all tokens within the tokenizer’s vocabulary. The other embedding layer stores all positional embeddings used in creating the model’s input.
Forward pass: Assuming we receive a tokenized sequence as input, we first retrieve all token embeddings and add positional embeddings to these token embeddings. After (optionally) applying dropout, we pass these token embeddings through the transformer blocks, then apply a final layer normalization. From here, we can either predict next tokens over all tokens in the sequence (pretraining) or on the last token (inference). Next tokens are predicted using a linear projection that outputs a vector with the same size as the vocabulary.
Generating text: If we want to generate a textual sequence, we just perform the forward pass defined above. However, we keep iteratively predicting the next token for the last token within the input sequence, adding it to our input sequence and repeating. This autoregressive process allows us to generate an entire sequence of text by just iteratively extending our input sequence by a single token.
Configuration: Notably, all of the settings within the architecture described above depend upon configured hyperparameters. For example, we can define the size of the token embeddings, the total number of blocks, the size of the model’s context window, and more by just tweaking the model’s configuration. To create a much larger language model, we typically just increase the embedding dimension and total number of layers. This approach is followed by most modern LLMs to increase model’s total number of parameters.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
One of the most widely-used forms of fine-tuning for LLMs is supervised fine-tuning (SFT). SFT is simple/cheap and a useful tool for aligning language models, which has made it popular for open-source LLM research and beyond…
Some history: The three-step alignment process—including both SFT and RLHF—was originally proposed by InstructGPT, the precursor and sister model to ChatGPT. Due to the success of ChatGPT, this three-step framework has become standardized and popular, leading to its use in a variety of LLMs (e.g., Sparrow and LLaMA-2). Alignment via SFT (and RLHF) is used heavily in both research and practical applications, and SFT is especially popular for open-source LLMs.
How does it work? For SFT, we curate a dataset of high-quality LLM outputs—these are basically just examples of the LLM behaving correctly. Then, we directly fine-tune the model on these examples using next token prediction. Here, the “supervised” aspect of fine-tuning comes from the fact that we are collecting a dataset of examples that the model should emulate.
The benefits. SFT is simple to use—the training process and objective are very similar to pretraining. Plus, the approach is highly effective at performing alignment and—relative to pretraining—is computationally cheap (i.e, 100X less expensive, if not more). Given its simplicity and effectiveness, SFT is a super popular technique for prototyping and fine-tuning LLMs.
SFT is not perfect. However, recent research indicates that performing RLHF on top of SFT yields a huge benefit. Plus, SFT requires the curation of a dataset with examples of good LLM outputs, which can be difficult and time consuming! The best way to ensure this dataset satisfies all alignment criteria is via manual inspection of quality and diversity.
Using SFT. One of the main reasons that SFT is so popular for open-source LLMs is due to its ease of use. Using the transformer reinforcement learning (TRL) package from HuggingFace, we can perform SFT on a pretrained model and public dataset with a few lines of code. SFT is simple to use, computationally inexpensive, and highly effective, making it a powerful tool for AI practitioners.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The RLAIF paper from Google has recently been a popular topic of discussion. The main idea (i.e.,scaling human preferences for RLHF with AI-provided feedback) is awesome, but my favorite part of the paper is the extensive prompting tips and takeaways that it provides…
TL;DR: Using generic LLMs to automate human preference feedback for RLHF is a powerful idea, but it requires an accurate and effective prompting approach to be developed. The recent RLAIF paper is a master class in test-driven prompting that arrives at a highly-accurate approach, making it a great resource for learning how to solve difficult problems with generic LLMs.
Some background: Reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) is nearly identical to reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), but it replaces the human feedback portion with feedback provided by a generic LLM. This LLM is prompted (using a template developed in [1]) to choose the LLM response that it prefers between two candidate responses.
AI Feedback: The basic prompt template used for generating preference feedback has four parts.
- Preamble: instructions that describe the task.
- Few-shot examples: (optional) examples of text with correct preference scores.
- Sample to annotate: input text and pair of summaries to be labeled with preference scores.
- Ending: ending string that prompts the model to generate preference scores (e.g., “Preferred Summary =”).
Then, the authors in [1] measure the log probability of each possible output (i.e., candidate LLM response 1 or 2) to generate a “soft” preference label between two candidate LLM responses.
CoT Prompting: Going beyond the basic template above, using CoT prompting yields a clear benefit in the accuracy of preference scores. Although this isn’t surprising (i.e., we already know that CoT prompting works well!), the approach used in [1] is a two-stage version of CoT prompting that first generates a rationale, concatenates this to the input, then generates a preference score. This two-stage approach is also used by multi-modal CoT [2] and graph of thoughts [3] prompting.
What doesn’t work? Using both few-shot learning and self-consistency [4] degrades the quality of preference scores. To me, this finding was really surprising! Self-consistency is not optimal due to taking a majority vote over model generations (i.e., approaches like DiVerse [5] or AMA [6] are better), but having it degrade performance compared to generating a single output is interesting. Plus, I haven’t seen many cases where few-shot learning actually made an LLM less accurate.
Other prompting tricks: Generic LLMs are subject to a number of different biases, such as position bias or recency bias. To protect against this, we can generate multiple outputs from the LLM with data positioned differently. In [1], this is done by generating two outputs with the position of candidate LLM responses flipped. Then, the final preference score is just an average of these two outputs, which prevents position/recency bias from impacting the preference score.
——
[1] Lee, Harrison, et al. “RLAIF: Scaling Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback with AI Feedback.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2309.00267 (2023).
[2] Zhang, Zhuosheng, et al. "Multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning in language models." arXiv preprint arXiv:2302.00923 (2023).
[3] Yao, Yao, Zuchao Li, and Hai Zhao. "Beyond Chain-of-Thought, Effective Graph-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models." arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.16582 (2023).
[4] Xuezhi Wang, Jason Wei, Dale Schuurmans, Quoc Le, Ed Chi, and Denny Zhou. 2022a. Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning in language models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2203.11171.
[5] Li, Yifei, et al. "On the advance of making language models better reasoners." arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.02336 (2022).
[6] Arora, Simran, et al. "Ask Me Anything: A simple strategy for prompting language models." arXiv preprint arXiv:2210.02441 (2022).

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
TopK sampling is a popular decoding strategy for language models, an alternative to options like TopP (nucleus sampling) or temperature, and a great way to control the randomness of a language model’s output. Here’s how it works…
Decoding process: To generate text with a language model, we begin with a (potentially empty) prefix (i.e., the prompt), then continually:
1. Generate the next token with the language model.
2. Add this next token to the current input/prefix.
3. Repeat.
This is an autoregressive process that iteratively selects each next token. See the attached image for a depiction and implementation (from Karpathy’s NanoGPT repository) of this process.
Selecting the next token: Instead of directly outputting the next token, language models output a probability distribution over the set of all possible tokens. Given this probability distribution, we can follow several different strategies for selecting the next token. For example, greedy decoding (one potential strategy) just selects the token with the highest probability as the next token!
How do we get these probabilities? Decoder-only transformers take a sequence of token vectors as input and produce a same-size list of vectors as output. For each token, we predict a probability distribution over next tokens via a linear layer that takes the token’s output vector as input and outputs a vector with the same size as the model’s vocabulary. By applying softmax (potentially with temperature), we can turn this vector into a probability distribution over tokens.
TopK Sampling has a hyperparameter TopK that determines how we sample. We take the TopK tokens with the highest probability, remove all other tokens, and renormalize the probability distribution (i.e., make sure probability of the TopK tokens sum to one). We only sample from these tokens, and the probability of sampling each token is proportional to its original probability.
Using TopK Sampling in Practice: TopK sampling can be controlled by setting the TopK parameter in most language model APIs. Notably, TopK is not present in the OpenAI API, but it is present for PaLM-2 and Claude. TopK can be used as an alternative to TopP and temperature for controlling the randomness of a model’s output. Unlike TopP sampling, TopK ensures that no single token is outputted with 100% probability by explicitly including TopK tokens in the sampling distribution.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is a powerful and necessary component of the alignment process. However, recent research has shown that RLHF can be made more scalable by automating human feedback with a generic language model…
TL;DR: RLHF is a powerful alignment tool, but it requires a large dataset of human preferences. Recent research like Constitutional AI (CAI) and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) mitigates this problem by using generic LLMs to automate the creation of preference datasets.
What is RLHF? RLHF finetunes an LLM based on human feedback. More specifically, we curate a human preference dataset by:
1. Obtaining a set of prompts
2. Generating two or more responses to each prompt with the LLM
3. Having a human annotator rank the responses based on preference
From the preference data outlined above, we can train a reward model that accurately predicts human preference given a response to a prompt. Then, we can finetune the LLM using a reinforcement learning algorithm (e.g., proximal policy optimization) to maximize the preference scores of its output, where the reward model is used to automate preference ratings.
Limitations of RLHF. Although RLHF contributed heavily to recent advancements in language models, it requires A LOT of human feedback data to work well. For example, LLaMA-2 uses roughly 100K examples for supervised fine-tuning. However, over 1M human preference examples are used for RLHF (i.e., an order of magnitude more data!).
“As AI systems become more capable, we would like to enlist their help to supervise other AIs.” - from Constitutional AI
How do we solve this? Obtaining human preference information is expensive and time consuming, but we have seen that LLMs are effective at generating their own training data (e.g., imitation models like Alpaca, self-instruct framework, or LLaMA-2). Going further, recent research has explored using generic LLMs to automate the human feedback portion of RLHF, making it more scalable and accessible.
Constitutional AI (CAI). Authors of CAI train a model that is helpful and harmless via alignment with SFT and RLHF. However, their approach leverages AI-provided feedback for collecting harmful preference data, both for SFT and RLHF. In particular, they write a set of 16 “principles” that together form a constitution that describes the properties of a harmless response. These principles are then used to critique examples for SFT and generate human preference feedback for RLHF.
RLAIF. Although CAI partially automates human feedback for alignment, the recently-proposed reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) paper completely automates human feedback. This is done, again, by prompting a generic LLM to generate feedback. Although RLAIF is only explored for text summarization tasks, it is found to produce models that perform quite well. Plus, advanced prompting techniques are found to improve the accuracy of AI-generated preference labels.

RLAIF: Scaling Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback with AI Feedback
paper page:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is effective at aligning large language models (LLMs) to human preferences, but gathering high quality human preference labels is a key bottleneck. We conduct a head-to-head comparison of RLHF vs. RL from AI Feedback (RLAIF) - a technique where preferences are labeled by an off-the-shelf LLM in lieu of humans, and we find that they result in similar improvements. On the task of summarization, human evaluators prefer generations from both RLAIF and RLHF over a baseline supervised fine-tuned model in ~70% of cases. Furthermore, when asked to rate RLAIF vs. RLHF summaries, humans prefer both at equal rates. These results suggest that RLAIF can yield human-level performance, offering a potential solution to the scalability limitations of RLHF.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Language models are powerful, but they have limitations. Integrating LLMs with specialized tools, which is one of the most promising directions of AI research, can make them 10X more effective. Here are the four different styles of tools being explored…
Basic tools. Tool usage for LLMs began with teaching models how to use basic tools, such as calculators or search engines. This was explored in the popular Toolformer paper, which fine-tunes a language model to exploit QA, search, and calculator tools when answering questions.
Deep Learning APIs. Another useful set of tools for language models are the APIs for deep learning models. Via platforms like HuggingFace and PyTorch, there are tons of specialized ML/AI models online that we can query via an API. Papers like HuggingGPT explored in-context learning or fine-tuning approaches to teach a language model to leverage these deep learning APIs.
Generic APIs. Beyond deep learning APIs, there are tons of other useful APIs available on the internet. Papers like Gorilla studied retrieval-aware fine-tuning approaches that teach a language model to retrieve documentation for relevant APIs and use this information to generate valid API requests. This was applied to deep learning APIs, but the approach is generally applicable.
LLM-generated tools. What do we do if the tool that we need is not available? One possibility would be to i) identify that we need a new tool to solve a problem and ii) use a generic language model to create the tool that is needed (e.g., via writing a prompt or code). This tool generation approach was studied by papers like LaTM and CREATOR.
The future. This area of research is rapidly evolving, so it’s hard to say exactly what tools will be useful for LLMs in the future. However, we learn from this area of research that delegating specialized skills to a tool and using the LLM as a general-purpose problem solver and aggregator of information can be incredibly effective.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Token embedding and classification layers consume tons of parameters within a language model. But, did you know that these layers can share their weights? This technique, called weight tying, actually improves the model’s performance…
Token embeddings. When we pass textual input to a language model, we first tokenize this input then look up a corresponding vector for each token. These vectors are stored in an embedding layer that contains a learnable vector for every token in the tokenizer’s vocabulary. This is a large number of vectors, which means that this embedding layer contains many parameters.
Token classification. After our input token vectors are passed through the language model, we receive a same-size list of output vectors. Then, we typically perform some classification, either of the next token (standard language modeling objective) or the masked token (masked language modeling objective). This classification layer, because it performs classification over the space of all possible tokens, is quite large.
Weight tying. To avoid consuming a ton of parameters within the token embedding and classification layers, we can use weight tying. This technique is quite simple—it just shares the parameters between the token embedding and classification layers. Interestingly, this technique not only reduces total parameters, but it improves the overall performance of the language model.
An implementation. For an example implementation of weight tying, we can look at Karpathy’s NanoGPT repository. The implementation is quite simple… we just set the weights of the token classification layer equal to the weights of the token embedding layer. Then, we can train our language model normally. Weight tying requires nothing extra or special!
Quick note. Although weight tying applies to generative LLMs, this technique was proposed in 2017 (i.e., well before GPT-3). As such, it applies to many different types of language models, including encoder-only models, neural translation models, and more. Token embedding and classification modules are present in a variety of different types of language models.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F6pz1NNWUAAjGdk.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Open LLM research is progressing rapidly, but existing efforts overemphasize supervised learning techniques and put less emphasis on reinforcement learning. One reason for this is that practitioners (including me) are simply less familiar with RL…
Disclaimer: We should note that there are several reasons people would rely more heavily on supervised learning than RL for LLM research. For example, RLHF requires human preference data to be curated and is generally less data efficient (needs a ton of data). However, top AI researchers admit a (perfectly reasonable) bias towards supervised learning techniques like SFT (see below).
“Many among us expressed a preference for supervised annotation, attracted by its denser signal… However, reinforcement learning proved highly effective, particularly given its cost and time effectiveness.” - from LLaMA-2
Why is RL necessary? We have seen that techniques like RLHF are super effective due to the role of alignment in creating state-of-the-art language models and the impact of RLHF on the alignment process. Top models like LLaMA-2 have demonstrated that the combination of both SFT and RLHF is important to create a foundation model that is performant and well-aligned.
Practitioners can (and should) learn RL! Despite these benefits, research in language models tends to learn towards supervised learning, partly because AI practitioners are more familiar with these techniques. But, learning RL is not horribly difficult. There are awesome packages out there (e.g., TRL from HuggingFace) that implement necessary tools, as well as datasets (e.g., HH-RLHF) available online for finetuning via RLHF. An in-depth understanding of RL broadens the scope of what we can build with LLMs.
Personal note: Despite working in AI/ML for the last 8 years, I have personally avoided learning about RL in detail, as it was never related to my work/research. LLMs have led me down the path of (finally) digging into RL research, and it’s reminded me how fun it is to learn new ideas from scratch. The breadth and pace of AI research is amazing. There’s always something new to learn, and that’s what I love about the space. Everyone is a beginner in some way or another.
