title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The gpt-oss models from OpenAI are a synthesis of ideas from prior research. Here are 10 interesting papers that were directly used in gpt-oss…
(1) Longformer: Introduces sliding window attention, a form of sparse attention that is utilized in alternating layers of both gpt-oss models.
(2) StreamingLLM: Describes the concept of attention sinks in large language models (LLMs)—these are tokens within a sequence that the model assigns high attention or weight to, simply because the softmax operation prevents the model from assigning attention to no tokens at all.
(3) Off-by-one attention: Proposes a solution to attention sinks by allowing the attention mechanism to assign no attention to any token. This is achieved by adding a bias term of 1 to the denominator of the softmax operation within attention. In gpt-oss models, a similar approach is used, but the bias term is learned rather than fixed at 1.
(4) Switch Transformer: Presents several ideas foundational to modern mixture-of-experts (MoE) based LLMs. It’s important to note that many other papers, in addition to Switch Transformer, have contributed to this field.
(5) RMSNorm: A streamlined variant of layer normalization that is both more efficient and has fewer trainable parameters. Both gpt-oss models employ RMSNorm.
(6) RoPE: Stands for Rotary Positional Encoding, a hybrid absolute/relative positional encoding method used by gpt-oss models. RoPE encodes absolute position using a rotation matrix and incorporates relative position information directly into the self-attention mechanism.
(7) YaRN: A method for extending the context window in LLMs, which is adopted by gpt-oss models. YaRN works by adjusting the frequency basis used within RoPE and further training the LLM to handle longer contexts.
(8) Flash Attention: Utilized by gpt-oss models, flash attention leverages system-level optimizations to significantly improve the computational and memory efficiency of the attention operation.
(9) DeepSeek-R1: While the specific reasoning or reinforcement learning (RL) training strategies used by gpt-oss models are not fully detailed, the DeepSeek-R1 technical report offers a comprehensive overview of how RL training with verifiable rewards is implemented at scale.
(10) Deliberative alignment: This is the safety training approach used by gpt-oss models, designed to teach the models how to reason through safety specifications and determine when it is appropriate to refuse a request.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GyWURhGWUAEhiA_.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
GPT-oss provides a rare peek into LLM research at OpenAI. Here are all of the technical details that OpenAI shared about the models…
(1) Model architecture. GPT-oss has two models in its family–20b and 120b. They both use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture. The 120b (20b) model has 128 (32) active experts and 5.1 (3.6) active parameters. Both models have four active experts in each MoE layer, which are chosen via a standard linear router.
Each block of GPT-oss models has 64 attention heads, and they models use GQA with a group size of 8. The layers alternate between using dense (masked) attention and locally banded sparse (also known as sliding window) attention with a window size of 128. They also use a new variant of off-by-one attention that adds a learnable bias into the denominator of the internal softmax of self-attention, which allows each attention head to pay attention to no tokens.
The models have an embedding dimension of 2,880 and adopt a pre-normalization block structure. RMSNorm is used for normalization in all transformer blocks. The feed-forward layers use a SwiGLU activation function. Both models use FlashAttention and expert-optimized triton kernels to improve training efficiency.
(2) Agentic Context Management. The GPT-oss models use OpenAI’s new Harmony prompt format, which is a great illustration of complex chat templates required by modern agentic LLMs. The Harmony format has five roles—system > developer > user > assistant > tool—that form a hierarchy in that order; e.g., developer message takes precedence over user message if there is a conflict. The assistant role has separate channels for tool calling, reasoning and final output. Put simply, the Harmony format integrates various agentic capabilities like tool calling, reasoning, structured outputs, multi-step instructions and more via a standard format.
“The model can interleave CoT, function calls, function responses, intermediate messages that are shown to users, and final answers.” - GPT-oss model card
(3) Long Context. The dense layers of GPT-oss have a (reasonably) long context length of 131K tokes. RoPE is used throughout the model, and authors perform context extension of both GPT-oss models to the 131K context length using YaRN—a targeted RoPE interpolation technique that extends NTK-by-parts interpolation by adding a temperature scaling parameter in the denominator of the softmax in self-attention.
(4) Model Training. The GPT-oss models have a knowledge cutoff of June 2024. They are trained on a text-only dataset (“trillions of tokens”) that is primarily English. Quantization-aware training with MXFP4 format (4.25 bits per parameter) is used to train the models, which makes them memory efficient. The 120b model can be hosted on a single 80Gb GPU, while the 20b model only requires ~16Gb memory for hosting. The models are first pretrained, then they undergo a cold start SFT phase focused on CoT reasoning followed by a high-compute RL stage (i.e., reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards). Deliberative alignment—a reasoning-centric safety training technique previously published by OpenAI and used to align all o-series models—is used for post-training GPT-oss models.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gyo3blcW8AAS1H5.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
My newsletter, Deep (Learning) Focus, recently passed 50,000 subscribers. Here are my four favorite articles and some reflections on my journey with the newsletter…
(1) Demystifying Reasoning Models outlines the key details of training reasoning-based LLMs, focusing on the details of the DeepSeek-R1 reasoning model. This overview covers key topics like verifiable rewards, RLVR and teaching LLMs to generate long chains of thought.
(2) AI Agents from First Principles provides a ground-up explanation of AI agents, beginning from the most basic concepts of LLMs. Starting with an explanation of next token prediction, we explain how LLMs–by using this basic functionality–can be generalized to perform tool use and reasoning, as well as how these techniques can be combined to create an open-ended agent.
(3) nanoMoE provides an in-depth explanation of how mixture-of-experts (MoEs) are used in LLM architectures. Based on the explanation, we create a from-scratch implementation of an MoE architecture in PyTorch. Additionally, we implement the entire pretraining process for a GPT-scale MoE and ablate various auxiliary losses and hyperparameter settings (e.g., precision level and weight initialization strategy) to eventually arrive at a stable training recipe.
(4) Using LLMs for Evaluation provides a comprehensive analysis of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation techniques. This overview presents a wide variety of different papers on this topic and ends with a practical discussion of how and when to use the many different setups that are available for LLM-as-a-Judge. A must read for anyone working on evals.
With this milestone, I’ve also spent some time reflecting on my journey with the newsletter.
The newsletter started during my PhD. When I read papers, I kept track of the papers I read in per-topic google documents with lists of papers on that topic with notes. Oftentimes, I combined these notes into a short essay that could be repurposed for related work in my papers. I wrote ~10 of these essays privately before publishing them online.
The current format of the newsletter goes beyond these simple writeups. My newsletters take ~40-50 hours to write, average ~10K words (oftentimes longer!), and are deeply technical. It regularly shocks me that people want to read such dense content. After publishing my first newsletter (on the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis), I told my wife that I just spent 50+ hours writing a 20 page essay that only 10 people will read if I’m lucky–what a waste of time!
Today, the newsletter receives hundreds of thousands of reads every month. But, I would still write it even if it was read by no one (I literally did this for years!). The value lies in the knowledge I gain from constantly reading papers and embarking on that difficult journey of writing a high-quality newsletter on a new topic every few weeks.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Is there truly a gap in performance between online and offline RL training for LLMs? Here’s what the research says…
TL;DR: There is a clear performance gap between online and offline RL algorithms, especially in large-scale LLM training. However, this gap can be minimized by incorporating on-policy samples into offline RL algorithms, creating an iterative or semi-online approach.
RL for LLMs: A few variants of RL (i.e., RLHF and RLVR) are used for training LLMs. These techniques differ in how they derive a reward, but they both operate by generating completions for a set of prompts, computing rewards for these completions, and using those rewards to update the LLM’s parameters via an RL optimizer.
RL optimizers: We usually use an (online) policy gradient-based RL optimizer (e.g., REINFORCE, PPO, or GRPO) to derive the policy update for an LLM. PPO-based RL has been the de facto choice in the past, but PPO:
- Is memory intensive due to storing four copies of the model (policy, reference, reward and critic / value models).
- Tends to be unstable and requires a lot of domain knowledge to set up correctly.
Plus, online RL is difficult due to the complexity of generating on-policy completions during training. Instead, we could use a simpler offline algorithm like DPO, as well as a semi-online algorithm like iterative DPO or rejection sampling.
(1) OOD data: In [1], the authors compare DPO with online RL algorithms, finding a clear bias in DPO. When DPO encounters out-of-distribution (OOD) or unseen responses, we see in [1] that the resulting LLM becomes biased toward these responses and behaves unpredictably. In contrast, PPO handles OOD data more robustly and learns a correct policy.
We can mitigate these issues with DPO by performing iterative / semi-online DPO, where we:
1. Collect new, on-policy completions from the current LLM.
2. Score them with a reward model to create preference pairs.
3. Run DPO on the new data.
4. Repeat.
(2) On-policy + negative gradient: Authors in [2] identify two key properties of alignment algorithms that lead to competitive performance:
1. On-policy sampling.
2. Negative gradients.
Online RL algorithms naturally contain on-policy sampling. We can also incorporate on-policy samples into offline or RL-free algorithms by including on-policy samples in the training data.
Negative gradients refer to the idea of pushing down the probability of “bad” completions. This naturally happens in PPO-based RL and DPO, but not in maximum likelihood algorithms like SFT.
(3) DPO vs. PPO at scale: Authors in [3] perform an extensive comparison between DPO and PPO-based RLHF with large-scale LLMs (i.e., 70B parameters), whereas prior work mostly focuses on smaller LLMs in experimental settings. In this work, we see a clear gap between the performance of DPO and PPO at scale. However, authors find that the quality of training data still has a bigger impact on LLM performance than algorithm choice (i.e., online vs. offline).
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G0Vl5toaAAEJ105.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The complexity of PPO leads practitioners to avoid online RL in favor of RL-free or offline algorithms (e.g., DPO), but why not just use simpler versions of online RL?
TL;DR: REINFORCE and RLOO have been shown to work well for training LLMs. And, they do not require a value model, which drastically reduces cost and complexity. Therefore, instead of completely avoiding online RL due to the overhead associated with PPO, we can just use algorithms that provide the benefits of online RL without the unnecessary complexity.
Policy gradient: RL optimizers operate by computing the gradient of the RL objective (maximizing rewards) w.r.t. policy parameters—this is called the policy gradient—and performing gradient ascent. A basic policy gradient is easy to compute (see figure) but has high variance. So, we introduce some extra complexity to get stable gradients / training.
Actor-critic: We can reduce variance by incorporating the advantage function (instead of the raw reward for a trajectory) into the policy gradient estimate. When we do this, the value function acts as a normalizer / baseline to the reward estimate for a state.
PPO estimates advantage with an additional copy of the LLM—called a value model or critic—that is trained via an MSE loss to predict the final reward for every token in a sequence. The critic is on-policy (i.e., it depends on the current parameters of the policy during training) and is trained alongside the policy itself during RL. This is called an actor-critic framework.
REINFORCE: Due to keeping and extra copy of the LLM in memory that is trained, actor-critic frameworks come with additional cost and complexity. As an alternative, we can use the much simpler REINFORCE algorithm, which estimates the value function via an average of rewards (either a moving average of all rewards or an average of rewards in a batch) throughout training. Estimating the value in this way is low cost and removes the need for a critic.
REINFORCE does yield higher variance relative to actor-critic methods, but recent work has shown that this does not matter in the context of LLMs. Algorithms like PPO were developed in a prior generation of DeepRL research, where neural networks were primarily trained from scratch. In the LLM domain, we are finetuning pretrained models with a strong prior—unstable gradients are much less of a worry. For this reason, even simple online RL algorithms like REINFORCE work well for training LLMs despite their higher variance.
RLOO: To reduce variance relative to REINFORCE, we can also use REINFORCE leave one out (RLOO). This algorithm reduces variance by sampling multiple completions for every prompt and estimating the value function as the average of rewards for other completions—excluding the completion for which the value is being estimated—to the same prompt.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
There are two common RL training formulations for LLMs: Markov Decision Process (MDP) formulation and bandit formulation. Here’s how they work…
Background: We should recall that an LLM generates output via next token prediction; i.e., by sequentially generating each output token. As shown in the image, the next token prediction process maps very easily to an RL setup—we can just model each token as an individual action!
MDP formulation: The approach of modeling each token in the LLM’s output as an individual action is called the Markov Decision Process (MDP) formulation. An MDP is simply a probabilistic framework for modeling decision-making that includes states, actions, transition probabilities and rewards—this is exactly the setup used by LLMs for RL!
Our initial state is the prompt and our policy acts by predicting tokens. During generation, actions are taken by selecting a token from the LLM’s predicted token distribution—each token is its own action. After a token is predicted, it is added to the current state and used by the LLM to predict the next token—this is just autoregressive next token prediction! Eventually, the LLM predicts a stop token (e.g., <|end_of_text|> or <eos>) to complete the generation process and yield a full trajectory.
Outcome vs process reward: In the MDP formulation, we depict a reward being provided to our policy at every step. But, the reward mechanism for an LLM is usually a bit different. Most LLMs are trained using outcome supervision, meaning that a reward is only assigned after the model has generated a complete response (i.e., after the <eos>).
Bandit formulation: In an outcome supervision setting, we may begin to question the utility of modeling each token as its own action. How do we handle credit assignment in this scenario? Alternatively, we could model the entire response as a single action that receives an outcome reward. This is the key idea behind the bandit formulation for RL training.
This name comes from the idea of a contextual bandit in probability theory. The bandit setup is simple: our agent chooses an action, receives a reward and the episode ends. Our complete trajectory is a single action and reward! For LLMs, our action is the full completion generated for a prompt, which receives an outcome reward.
Which formulation is better? In the context of LLMs, we can easily compute the probability of either individual tokens or a full completion to a prompt, so we have the ability to model RL using either an MDP or bandit formulation. Given that LLMs usually only receive outcome rewards, however, the bandit formulation—despite being very simple—is quite fitting for LLMs. Plus, it tends to be more simple (and has been argued to perform similarly despite this simplicity). However, MDP formulations are also commonly used. For example, PPO uses an MDP formulation, whereas REINFORCE and RLOO adopt a bandit formulation. In other words, both RL formulations are viable and are used for training LLMs.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is one of the most common (and complicated) RL algorithms used for LLMs. Here’s how it works…
TRPO. PPO is inspired by TRPO, which uses a constrained objective that:
1. Normalizes action / token probabilities of current policy by those of an old policy from before training. This forms a policy ratio.
2. Constrains the average KL divergence between new and old policies to be less than δ.
The constrained objective in TRPO is guaranteed to improve monotonically, but it is is complicated to solve practically.
From TRPO to PPO. We want an algorithm with the benefits of TRPO—e.g., stability, data efficiency, and reliability—but without its complexity. PPO’s objective is inspired by the TRPO but replaces the hard KL constraint with a clipping mechanism to enforce a trust region in a simpler way.
PPO training process. PPO goes beyond a single policy update in each step, alternating between:
1. Sampling new data or trajectories from the policy.
2. Performing several (usually 2-4 for LLMs) policy updates over the sampled data.
Clipped objective. We start with the TRPO objective with no constraint (unclipped objective). We then introduce a clipped objective that is the same as the unclipped objective but clips the policy ratio to be in the range [1 - ε, 1 + ε]. PPO takes the minimum of clipped and unclipped objectives, making it a lower bound for the unclipped objective.
The behavior of clipping changes based on the sign of the advantage (i.e., clipping is only applied in one direction). We can arbitrarily decrease the objective via the policy ratio, but we are restricted from increasing it. This allows PPO to de-incentivize large policy ratios and enforce a trust region.
KL divergence. We incorporate a KL divergence between the current policy and a reference policy (e.g., the SFT model) when training LLMs with PPO to avoid the policy becoming too different from the reference. We compute KL divergence per token by comparing token probability distributions from the two LLMs for each token in the sequence. This can be added as a penalty to the PPO loss or directly subtracted from the reward.
The critic. The last step in PPO is computing the advantage, which is the difference between the state-action value function and the value function. We estimate the state-action value function (i.e., expected reward for a specific action in a given state) with the actual reward. The value function is estimated with a learned model called the critic or value model.
Unlike a reward model that predicts the outcome reward, the critic predicts expected reward per token. The value function is also on-policy, unlike reward models which are fixed at the beginning of RL training. In PPO, the critic is trained alongside the LLM in each policy update by using an MSE loss against actual / observed rewards. This is called an actor-critic setup.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Let’s implement Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) together…
Step #1 - Rollouts. We begin the PPO policy update with a batch of prompts. Using our current policy (i.e., the LLM we are training), we sample a single completion for each of these prompts. Additionally, we will predict a reward for each completion with our reward model.
Step #2 - Logprobs. We compute the log probabilities for every token in every completion of our batch using both the current policy and our reference model, which is usually the SFT model or some other model checkpoint prior to RL training.
Step #3 - KL divergence. We compute the KL divergence between the current policy and the reference policy. In this implementation, we use the simplest approximation / estimator for the KL divergence, which takes the difference in logprobs between the policy and reference. See [1] for an overview of different techniques for estimating KL divergence.
In PPO, the KL divergence is directly incorporated into the reward after being scaled by the coefficient β. In other algorithms (e.g., GRPO), the KL divergence is instead added as a penalty to the loss.
Step #4 - Advantage. The value function in PPO is predicted by a value model / critic. The critic is another copy of the LLM—trained alongside the policy itself—that predicts expected future rewards for each token. The critic is similar to a reward model, but it predicts expected reward on a per-token basis.
In this implementation, the advantage is estimated as the difference between rewards and values predicted by the critic. This is a basic / simplified approach—we would use GAE in practice [2].
Step #5 - PPO loss. We compute the surrogate loss for PPO next by:
1. Computing the policy ratio between the current and old policies.
2. Computing the clipped version of this policy ratio.
3. Using these two terms to compute the minimum of the clipped and unclipped PPO objective.
Step #6 - Composite loss. We are training both the policy and the critic simultaneously. The critic is trained using an MSE loss between predicted and actual rewards. We compute this MSE loss, scale it by coefficient critic_weight, and combine the losses for the critic and PPO to train both of these models simultaneously. We must also aggregate the loss over the batch prior to performing the final policy update.
Once the losses have been computed, we just perform a gradient update for our policy and our critic using standard PyTorch syntax. Usually, we perform several updates over a single batch of data in PPO. The old model is the model at the beginning of these several updates, and it is updated each time we sample new data.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE)–used in PPO–is one of the most complicated aspects of reinforcement learning (RL). Here’s how it works and how we can implement it…
The advantage tells us how much better a given action is compared to the average action in a given state: A(s_t, a_t) = Q(s_t, a_t) - V(s_t). In PPO, we estimate the value function V(s_t) with a learned critic model. The advantage function is estimated on a per-token (or action) basis.
Temporal Difference (TD). The TD residual is one way of estimating the advantage. It uses per-token value predictions (from the critic) to form a one-step advantage estimate. This TD residual analyzes how much the expected reward changes after predicting a single token.
By using the actual reward r_t, the TD residual incorporates some exact information into our advantage estimate—the terms in the estimate come partly from our critic and partly from real rewards. Using token-level rewards to estimate the advantage lowers the variance of the policy gradient. If our value function were exact, then the TD residual would also be unbiased. But, the fact that we are using a learned value model makes the TD residual biased.
N-step estimators. The TD residual analyzes the difference between actual and expected reward for a single step. We can generalize this idea to capture any number of steps by forming an N-step advantage estimator with a similar structure to the TD residual. However, this estimator incorporates real rewards for N states, where N can be greater than one.
Similarly to the TD residual, estimators with lower N have low variance but high bias. Increasing N incorporates more exact reward information, which lowers the bias (and increases variance).
Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE), the most commonly-used approach for estimating the advantage in PPO, makes use of N-step advantage estimates. Instead of choosing a single value of N, however, GAE takes an average of all possible N-step advantage estimates.
This is done by introducing a mixing parameter λ ∈ [0, 1] for GAE, which controls the tradeoff between bias and variance. As we increase the value of λ, more exact reward information is used in the advantage estimate, thus lowering the bias (but increasing variance). Similarly, we can use lower values of λ to reduce variance at the cost of higher bias.
Implementation. We can efficiently compute the GAE recursion by iterating through the sequence in reverse order. For a concrete example, we provide a code snippet from GAE computation in the PPO script from Ai2’s OpenInstruct repo (see image).

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The Olmo technical reports / artifacts are by far the most useful resource for those working on LLMs outside of closed frontier labs. You can read the papers, read the code, look at the data, and even train the models yourself. No other resource provides this level of detail, and the models are all openly available (with a massive improvement over Olmo-2 / Tulu-3) to start using now.
Quoting @natolambert
We present Olmo 3, our next family of fully open, leading language models.
This family of 7B and 32B models represents:
1. The best 32B base model.
2. The best 7B Western thinking & instruct models.
3. The first 32B (or larger) fully open reasoning model.
This is a big milestone for Ai2 and the Olmo project. These aren’t huge models (more on that later), but it’s crucial for the viability of fully open-source models that they are competitive on performance – not just replications of models that came out 6 to 12 months ago. As always, all of our models come with full training data, code, intermediate checkpoints, training logs, and a detailed technical report. All are available today, with some more additions coming before the end of the year.
As with OLMo 2 32B at its release, OLMo 3 32B is the best open-source language model ever released. It’s an awesome privilege to get to provide these models to the broader community researching and understanding what is happening in AI today.
Base models – a strong foundation
Pretraining’s demise is now regularly overstated. 2025 has marked a year where the entire industry rebuilt their training stack to focus on reasoning and agentic tasks, but some established base model sizes haven’t seen a new leading model since @alibaba_qwen's Qwen 2.5 in 2024. The Olmo 3 32B base model could be our most impactful artifact here, as Qwen3 did not release their 32B base model (likely for competitive reasons). We show that our 7B recipe competes with Qwen 3, and the 32B size enables a starting point for strong reasoning models or specialized agents. Our base model’s performance is in the same ballpark as Qwen 2.5, surpassing the likes of Stanford’s Marin (@stanfordAILab) and Gemma 3 (@GoogleDeepMind), but with pretraining data and code available, it should be more accessible to the community to learn how to finetune it (and be confident in our results).
We’re excited to see the community take Olmo 3 32B base in many directions. 32B is a loved size for easy deployment on single 80GB+ memory GPUs and even on many laptops, like the MacBook I’m using to write this on.
A model flow – the lifecycle of creating a model
With these strong base models, we’ve created a variety of post-training checkpoints to showcase the many ways post-training can be done to suit different needs. We’re calling this a “Model Flow.” For post-training, we’re releasing Instruct versions – short, snappy, intelligent, and useful especially for synthetic data en masse (e.g. recent work by Datology @datologyai on OLMo 2 Instruct), Think versions – thoughtful reasoners with the performance you expect from a leading thinking model on math, code, etc. and RL Zero versions – controlled experiments for researchers understanding how to build post-training recipes that start with large-scale RL on the base model.
The first two post-training recipes are distilled from a variety of leading, open and closed, language models. At the 32B and smaller scale, direct distillation with further preference finetuning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is becoming an accessible and highly capable pipeline. Our post-training recipe follows our recent models: 1) create an excellent SFT set, 2) use direct preference optimization (DPO) as a highly iterable, cheap, and stable preference learning method despite its critics, and 3) finish up with scaled up RLVR. All of these stages confer meaningful improvements on the models’ final performance.
Instruct models – low latency workhorse
Instruct models today are often somewhat forgotten, but the likes of @aiatmeta Llama 3.1 Instruct and smaller, concise models are some of the most adopted open models of all time. The instruct models we’re building are a major polishing and evolution of the Tülu 3 pipeline – you’ll see many similar datasets and methods, but with pretty much every datapoint or training code being refreshed. Olmo 3 Instruct should be a clear upgrade on Llama 3.1 8B, representing the best 7B scale model from a Western or American company. As scientists we don’t like to condition the quality of our work based on its geographic origins, but this is a very real consideration to many enterprises looking to open models as a solution for trusted AI deployments with sensitive data.
Building a thinking model
What people have most likely been waiting for are our thinking or reasoning models, both because every company needs to have a reasoning model in 2025, but also to clearly open the black box for the most recent evolution of language models. Olmo 3 Think, particularly the 32B, are flagship models of this release, where we considered what would be best for a reasoning model at every stage of training.
Extensive effort (ask me IRL about more war stories) went into every stage of the post-training of the Think models. We’re impressed by the magnitude of gains that can be achieved in each stage – neither SFT nor RL is all you need at these intermediate model scales.
First we built an extensive reasoning dataset for supervised finetuning (SFT), called Dolci-Think-SFT, building on very impactful open projects like OpenThoughts3, Nvidia’s Nemotron Post-training, Prime Intellect’s SYNETHIC-2, and many more open prompt sources we pulled forward from Tülu 3 / OLMo 2. Datasets like this are often some of our most impactful contributions (see the Tülu 3 dataset as an example in Thinking Machine’s Tinker :D @thinkymachines @tinker_api – please add Dolci-Think-SFT too, and Olmo 3 while you’re at it, the architecture is very similar to Qwen which you have).
For DPO with reasoning, we converged on a very similar method as HuggingFace’s (@huggingface) SmolLM 3 with Qwen3 32B as the chosen model and Qwen3 0.6B as the rejected. Our intuition is that the delta between the chosen and rejected samples is what the model learns from, rather than the overall quality of the chosen answer alone. These two models provide a very consistent delta, which provides way stronger gains than expected. Same goes for the Instruct model. It is likely that DPO is helping the model converge on more stable reasoning strategies and softening the post-SFT model, as seen by large gains even on frontier evaluations such as AIME.
Our DPO approach was an expansion of Geng, Scott, et al. "The delta learning hypothesis: Preference tuning on weak data can yield strong gains." arXiv preprint arXiv:2507.06187 (2025). Many early open thinking models that were also distilled from larger, open-weight thinking models likely left a meaningful amount of performance on the table by not including this stage.
Finally, we turn to the RL stage. Most of the effort here went into building effective infrastructure to be able to run stable experiments with the long-generations of larger language models. This was an incredible team effort to be a small part of, and reflects work ongoing at many labs right now. Most of the details are in the paper, but our details are a mixture of ideas that have been shown already like ServiceNow’s PipelineRL or algorithmic innovations like DAPO and Dr. GRPO. We have some new tricks too!
Some of the exciting contributions of our RL experiments are 1) what we call “active refilling” which is a way of keeping the generations from the learner nodes constantly flowing until there’s a full batch of completions with nonzero gradients (from equal advantages) – a major advantage of our asynchronous approach; and 2) cleaning, documenting, decontaminating, mixing, and proving out the large swaths of work done by the community over the last months.
The result is an excellent model that we’re very proud of. It has very strong reasoning benchmarks (AIME, GPQA, etc.) while also being stable, quirky, and fun in chat with excellent instruction following. The 32B range is largely devoid of non-Qwen competition. The scores for both of our Thinkers get within 1-2 points overall with their respective Qwen3 8/32B models – we’re proud of this!
A very strong 7B scale, Western thinking model is Nvidia’s (@NVIDIAAI) NVIDIA-Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2 hybrid model. It came out months ago and is extremely strong. I personally suspect it may be due to the hybrid architecture making subtle implementation bugs in popular libraries, but who knows.
All in, the Olmo 3 Think recipe gives us a lot of excitement for new things to try in 2026.
RL Zero
DeepSeek R1 showed us a way to new post-training recipes for frontier models, starting with RL on the base model rather than a big SFT stage (yes, I know about cold-start SFT and so on, but that’s an implementation detail). We used RL on base model as a core feedback cycle when developing the model, such as during intermediate midtraining mixing. This is viewed now as a fundamental, largely innate, capability of the base-model.
To facilitate further research on RL Zero, we released 4 datasets and series of checkpoints, showing per-domain RL Zero performance on our 7B model for data mixes focus on math, code, instruction following, and all mixed together.
In particular, we’re excited about the future of RL Zero research on Olmo 3 precisely because everything is open. Researchers can study the interaction between the reasoning traces we include at midtraining and the downstream model behavior (qualitative and quantitative).
This helps answer questions that have plagued RLVR results on Qwen models, hinting at forms of data contamination particularly on math and reasoning benchmarks (see Shao, Rulin, et al. "Spurious rewards: Rethinking training signals in rlvr." arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.10947 (2025). or Wu, Mingqi, et al. "Reasoning or memorization? unreliable results of reinforcement learning due to data contamination." arXiv preprint arXiv:2507.10532 (2025).)
What’s next
This is the biggest project we’ve ever taken on at Ai2 (@allen_ai), with 60+ authors and numerous other support staff.
In building and observing “thinking” and “instruct” models coming today, it is clear to us that there’s a very wide variety of models that fall into both of these buckets. The way we view it is that thinking and instruct characteristics are on a spectrum, as measured by the number of tokens used per evaluation task. In the future we’re excited to view this thinking budget as a trade-off, and build models that serve different use-cases based on latency/throughput needs.
As for a list of next models or things we’ll build, we can give you a list of things you’d expect from a (becoming) frontier lab: MoEs, better character training, pareto efficient instruct vs think, scale, specialized models we actually use at Ai2 internally, and all the normal things.
This is one small step towards what I see as a success for my ATOM project.
We thank you for all your support of our work at Ai2. We have a lot of work to do. We’re going to be hunting for top talent at NeurIPS to help us scale up our Olmo team in 2026.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The original PPO-based RLHF pipeline had 4 model copies:
1. Policy
2. Reference
3. Critic
4. Reward Model
Recent GRPO-based RLVR pipelines have eliminated all of these models except for the policy.
- The critic is no longer needed because values are estimated from group statistics.
- We use verifiable rewards (no need for a reward model).
Reasoning RL / RLVR pipelines are removing kl divergence. It's cool that this can be done without training instability, but I recently realized this also means means we no longer need a reference model (reference is only used for kl approximation). So, we've removed yet another model from RL training.
RL training for LLMs may be one of the few research areas that has actually moved towards simplicitly over time rather than complexity.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Looking for something to talk to your family about this Thanksgiving? How about the implementation details of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)? Here’s how it works…
(1) On-policy completions. We begin with a diverse batch of B prompts. Using our current policy, we sample a group of G—where G >> 1—completions for each prompt. GRPO uses large batches; e.g., DeepSeek-Math uses B = 16 and G = 64 for a total batch size of 1,024.
(2) Outcome rewards. Next, we compute the reward for each completion in our batch. GRPO is often used in tandem with verifiable rewards to train reasoning models. In this scenario, our reward is assigned to the whole completion based on correctness (e.g., binary pass-fail reward), but GRPO can also be generalized to process-level rewards.
(3) Log probabilities. We then compute the log probability of each token in each completion using both our current policy and the reference policy (e.g., the SFT model). These probabilities are used to compute the KL divergence and the probability ratio in the GRPO loss.
(4) KL divergence. We also compute an approximation of the KL divergence between the policy and reference policy. There are three main techniques for approximating KL divergence (called k_1, k_2, and k_3 in John Schulman’s blog post on the topic). Both k_1 and k_3 are shown in this implementation. k_1 is a common and simple approximation used by LLMs, but k_3—which is more complicated but has lower variance—is usually used for GRPO because it was originally used by DeepSeek-Math (i.e., the paper that proposed GRPO).
(5) Advantage. To compute advantage, we first compute the mean and standard deviation of rewards in each group. The advantage for completion i is then computed by subtracting the mean reward of the group from the completion’s reward r_i and dividing by the standard deviation of rewards in the group. Advantage is estimated based on rewards for different completions to the same prompt—each token in a completion gets the same advantage.
(6) Surrogate loss. GRPO uses the same surrogate loss function from Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which takes the product of the policy ratio (between the current policy and a snapshot of the policy prior to the first update of this batch) and the advantage. We also adopt the same clipping mechanism used by PPO, which constrains the policy ratio to be in the range [1 - ε, 1 + ε]. We then compute the loss function both with and without clipping and take their minimum.
Unlike PPO, GRPO also incorporates the KL divergence as a penalty term into the loss function (instead of directly subtracting it from the reward). However, KL divergence terms are generally becoming less common for training reasoning models—this term could be omitted.
(7) Update. From here, we can simply call .backward() on our loss to compute the policy gradient and update our policy.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The swarm optimization approach used by Olmo-3 to discover good pretraining data mixtures is super cool.
It runs a guided search over possible data mixtures by:
1. Randomly sampling a bunch of mixtures.
2. Training small-scale proxy models on these mixtures.
3. Evaluating the proxy models.
4. Training per-task regression models to predict eval results from mixing coefficients / ratios.
5. Running a constrained optization to find the mixture that maximizes performance while meeting data constraints (e.g., max tokens or re-sampling).
The above steps form a base procedure for data mixing. We can also perform iterative data mixing during model development via conditional mixing.
Data sources are constantly changing during the model development process. Instead of re-running our mix optimization procedure from scratch, we can:
- Start with an existing optimized mix.
- Treat this mix as a "virtual" source with a fixed ratio.
- Optimize the mix only over new / changed sources.
I love the gradient-free optimization techniques being used for LLMs! Evolution / swarm techniques have so much potential for meta-learning.
Also, the level of practical details in this paper is insane. It is one of the most useful and information dense papers written on LLMs in quite some time.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7Ipt4kWYAAbF5g.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Easy to miss because it's on the last page of the paper, but Olmo 3 RL-Zero has a really nice sub-section on RL with random rewards!
Prior papers (Shao et al - "Spurious Rewards: Rethinking Training Signals in RLVR") show RLVR still improves performance on math problems even when we assign completely random rewards to model completions. This was a weird result that raised a lot of questions on how RLVR actually works.
There are several explanations for why this might happen:
- GRPO reinforces existing model tendencies (e.g., generating code in the output) that may be conducive to math problem solving.
- Data contamination.
- Most of these results are observed with Qwen-2.5, so this particular model could have unknown data / model properties that cause this to happen.
The authors of Olmo 3 show that this random improvement property of RLVR disappears with proper data decontamination. If we ensure no downstream evaluation data is present in our pretraining or midtraining datasets, then RL training with random rewards no longer yields any performance improvement.
Such an observation really highlights how important fully open models are for conducting rigorous research. Without any knowledge of a model's training data, we can unknowingly observe seemingly surprising trends that may be a result of data contamination / leakage rather than something substantial.
Olmo 3 RL-Zero seems to be an awesome and clean test bed for running RL experiments:
- Base model is already openly available.
- Multi-objective / several tasks
- Simple chat templates are tested and provided for each task
- Full data transparency, data is decontaminated
- Predefined recipes (with open code) that already perform well are provided as a baseline
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7tW55ubIAA9uVi.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Some more thoughts on RLVR with random rewards and why random / incorrect rewards still boost performance…
The primary training setup for this paper was a Qwen-2.5 base model on Math-500 (i.e., the new “hello world” problem for RLVR). Notably, Qwen-2.5 is not a reasoning model and was released early enough to not be trained on long CoT data. However, there is some evidence that Qwen-2.5 models were trained on tool / math data that benefits downstream reasoning performance.
The paper that observed the phenomenon of improved math capabilities with RLVR from random rewards didn’t just use random rewards, they tested out all of the following:
- Actual / ground truth reward (standard RLVR setup): +24.6 on Math 500
- Majority vote from multiple completions: +23.2 on Math 500
- Run RLVR on one training example: +21.4 on Math 500
- Incorrect label (i.e., literally rewarding model for wrong answers): +21.2 on Math 500
- Random rewards: +15.8 on Math 500
We see above that providing some meaningful reward signal (even if just a single example) still yields a much bigger benefit than random rewards. But, what’s shocking about these results is:
1. Random rewards still yield a benefit.
2. Incorrect rewards yield an even bigger benefit!
Notably, these results were almost purely observed with Qwen-2.5, indicating that this might be a unique property of this particular RLVR setup (i.e., model and task combination) instead of a fundamental property of RLVR. One possible explanation for this behavior is that some data contamination exists with Qwen-2.5 for the Math 500 benchmark, which is (partially) confirmed in analysis from Olmo 3. Specifically, Olmo 3 shows that after decontaminating midtraining / pretraining data, we no longer see a performance benefit from RLVR with random rewards.
“When using spurious rewards the rate of code reasoning strategies shifts from ~65% on the base model to 90%+ after RLVR.” - from Spurious Rewards: Rethinking Training Signals in RLVR
Beyond data contamination, there is also another explanation for why RLVR with random rewards benefits math performance in this setup:
- Qwen models are very good at generating code to assist in math reasoning problems (even with no code execution). Code reasoning has been correlated with math performance, and RLVR (even with random rewards) increases the likelihood of code reasoning for Qwen.
- In the DAPO paper, authors also observe entropy with PPO / GRPO decreases quickly during training (i.e., token distributions become more concentrated / confident so outputs tend to be similar if you sample multiple times). This is due to the fact that clipping in PPO restricts policy updates for low probability tokens more than for high probability tokens due to the structure of the policy ratio.
- To solve this issue, DAPO recommends the clip higher approach - just increase the upper bound of the clipping range in PPO so that clipping is not too restrictive of policy updates.
- Specifically, what is happening in the case of RLVR with random rewards is that the clipping mechanism is reducing entropy quickly and reinforcing existing behavior in the model. For example, clipping could reinforce the behavior of Qwen-2.5 to perform code reasoning for solving math problems and, in turn, improve its performance.
Considering all of these observations, the RLVR from random rewards paper also tried to remove clipping from GRPO to see if this has an impact — and it does. Without clipping, we no longer see a performance improvement with random rewards!
Given this analysis and recent results from Olmo 3, we can’t say that RLVR from random rewards is entirely a product of data contamination. After all, Olmo 3 uses the clip higher trick from DAPO, which should mitigate issues with random rewards even for contaminated models! This phenomenon probably comes form a combination of data / model issues (including some level of contamination) and random impacts from small practical settings in RL.
There are many small details an heuristics present in RL pipelines today (e.g., aggregation strategy for the loss, importance sampling, clipping, advantage formulation, etc.) that all can have unexpected impacts on performance or biases. Additionally, we can induce weird behavior by how we specify the reward! In fact, one of the authors of the RLVR with random rewards paper even mentioned an experiment where they observed improved performance on Math 500 just by penalizing incomplete responses and nothing else.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Curious about how reinforcement learning (RL) actually works for reasoning models / LLMs? Olmo 3 Think provides a fully-open pipeline for trying this out yourself…
Starting with a base (pretrained) model, we first perform supervised finetuning (SFT) over a dataset of ~2.3M supervised examples with reasoning traces. This data is sourced from public datasets like Open Thoughts 3 and Synthetic 2. However, Olmo 3 further filters this data based on correctness, topic relevance, and some hand-crafted heuristics.
Although most reasoning models forgo preference tuning, Olmo 3 runs Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) prior to RL training. To construct preference pairs, a Delta Learning approach is used, which creates preference pairs by sampling:
- A chosen completion from a good model (Qwen-3-32B).
- A rejected completion from a lower-quality model (Qwen-3-0.6B).
Interestingly, Olmo 3 shows that using both SFT and DPO in tandem—if careful attention is paid to data curation—is a better starting point for RL compared to just SFT or performing RL directly on the base model.
Finally, Olmo 3 undergoes Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a standard RL setup for reasoning models.
Instead of using vanilla GRPO, Olmo 3 adopts a variety of algorithmic tweaks inspired by recent work on the topic:
- Zero Gradient Filtering: prompts for which the entire group of completions or rollouts in GRPO receive the same reward are removed.
- Active Sampling: a constant batch size is maintained by ensuring additional samples are always available to replace those that get filtered.
- Token-Level Loss: the GRPO loss is normalized by the total number of tokens across the batch instead of per-sequence.
- No KL: the KL divergence term is removed from the GRPO loss to allow for more flexibility in the policy updates.
- Clipping Upper Bound: the upper-bound term in the PPO-style clipping used by GRPO is set higher than the lower bound.
- Truncated Importance Sampling (TIS): an importance sampling term is added to the GRPO loss to adjust for deltas in logprobs between training / rollout engines.
- No Standard Deviation: the standard deviation of rewards is removed from the denominator of the GRPO advantage.
Standard verifiers are used for math and code. Unlike most recent work on RLVR, however, the model is also trained on general chat data, where an LLM judge—with or without a reference—provides the reward signal. By training on this mixture of rewards, Olmo 3 achieves near (but slightly behind) state-of-the-art performance and maintains general capabilities.
Authors continue running RL for 3 weeks after the model release, and the model continues to improve without any training instability, indicating that this RLVR recipe is stable and functional. If you want to try it yourself, all code, data, evaluations and technical details for the entire Olmo 3 training process are openly provided by authors at AI2!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G8PY8BTWEAAYMrF.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
One fun detail about Olmo 3: the 7b model uses regular multi-headed self-attention, but the 32b model uses GQA.
Nathan discusses the reasons for this in his recent Olmo 3 Think talk:
- Olmo 3 started with the Qwen-2.5 architecture.
- When they reached the RL training phase, inference (and therefore training) was too slow.
- The change to GQA in the 32B model was done to speed up inference for RL.
- The boost in inference efficiency from GQA made RL way faster because 75% of the time is spent on rollouts.
Great example of how fundamental architectural details that you would think are mostly relevant to pretraining are still important to consider even at the final phase of post-training! It pays to understand the full stack.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The truncated importance sampling (TIS) RL paper / blog was extended with a lot of extra analysis a few months ago. One of the most interesting tidbits was that using TIS (despite having a huge performance benefit) tends to decrease rewards during training. However, this is simply a logging artifact. Here's why it happens...
In efficient RL frameworks, we use two separate engines:
1. Sampler engine (based on vLLM / SGLang) to compute rollouts.
2. Learner engine (based on FSDP / DeepSpeed / other distributed training framework) to compute policy updates.
The sampler engine is very fast because it uses modern optimized inference engines. Given that most of the cost of RL training is spent on inference, the sampler needs to be extremely fast. But, this efficiency comes at a cost - there tends to be a mismatch between these engines. The token probabilities will be slightly different between the sampler / learner, thus making the RL training process slightly off policy. This mismatch persists even when engineering effort is invested into minimizing differences between the engines.
Truncated importance sampling (TIS) fixes this by scaling the policy gradient by a capped importance ratio (directly taken from the statistical definition of importance sampling). This approach corrects for the engine mismatch - and, in turn, improves model performance - and has been validated practically in several papers that cite TIS as essential for scaling RL.
However, if we add TIS to our RL training process, we might notice that the reward being logged during training becomes slightly lower, even when the final model performs better. This phenomenon occurs because the reward being logged during training is derived from our rollouts, which come from the sampler engine. The sampler is the proxy distribution for TIS, while the learner is the target distribution.
The purpose of TIS is to adjust the policy gradient to account for the mismatch between these distributions. By reweighting gradient contributions with a (truncated) importance ratio, the update better approximates the on-policy gradient of the learner, even though data is collected from the sampler. Learning is guided by the learner’s expected return rather than being biased toward regions overrepresented by the sampler. As a result, the reward observed for the sampler might actually be slightly lower compared to a run that does not use TIS, but the learner's reward / policy performance benefits from using TIS.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G9Za3MVWgAE6f3o.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G9Za6AMXYAATKFf.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Another interesting contribution from TIS is a practical analysis of what contributes to the mismatch between rollouts and policy updates in RL. We see in particular that:
- The choice of inference backend (e.g., vllm or sglang) does not have a huge impact.
- Using different distribution strategies between sampling and policy updates (e.g., tensor versus sequence parallelism) worsens the mismatch.
- Using different settings for the same kind of parallelism (e.g., tensor parallelism with 4 versus 8 GPUs) is less detrimental compared to a completely different distribution strategy.
- The length of the rollout significatly impacts the mismatch (i.e., longer sequences have a bigger gap).
This is measured using a fixed set of example prompts. For each prompt, they measure the mean and max difference in token probabilities (between the rollout and the policy update) across the sequence. In most cases, mean mismatch is the same, but there is an increase in outlier tokens with large probability discrepancies. Therefore, the mismatch is most visible in terms of the max probability discrepancy metric.

summary:
I published 154,434 words (~1.5 books) across 16 newsletters that were read by ~300,000 people in 2025. None of these words were written by an LLM. Here’s why…
LLM research moves quickly. It seems that every few months the field completely reinvents itself. In order to keep pace, researchers (including me) must constantly evolve their skill sets.
Due to this fast pace, I set a goal to prioritize skill acquisition at the beginning of the year. As my career has gotten busier, this goal has become more difficult. However, I set strict deadlines for publishing my newsletter that force me to allocate time to learning.
Strict deadlines cause a lot of mental friction. I’ve had many 60 to 80 hour work weeks turned into 100+ hour work weeks as I try to finish my newsletter on nights / weekends. “He’s trying to finish his newsletter” has become a sarcastic trope among my family.
Despite the process being difficult, the newsletter has deepened my understanding of so many different topics (e.g., RL, MoEs, VLMs, agents, new models, recent trends in post-training, etc.). Gaining this level of understanding without going through the process of planning and writing each newsletter would be impossible.
Given the time I’ve invested and the quality bar I’ve upheld, I am very proud of the newsletter and its reach, but I am most proud of what I have learned. The newsletter has allowed me to improve as a researcher, engineer and teacher.
Going into 2026, I’m primarily motivated by what I don’t know. As I continue writing, I’ll barely scratch the surface of our collective and expanding understanding of AI research. I look forward to learning new things and remaining curious!

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Geometric mean policy optimization (GMPO) is a really interesting GRPO variant.
One of the key issues with GRPO is that we use outcome rewards, but the loss function includes a token-level importance ratio. Throughout training, the magnitude of these importance ratios increases a lot. This leads to outlier importance values and, in turn, unstable policy gradients.
Instead of combatting this issue via clipping like GRPO / PPO and most of their variants, GMPO tries to improve stability by using a different strategy for aggregating the loss over the sequence.
GRPO uses an arithmetic mean to aggregate token level losses over the sequence (i.e., the loss for the sequence is average of losses for each token). This works poorly because arithmetic means are sensitive to outliers. So we get:
outlier importance values --> outlier token-level losses --> unstable / high-variance policy gradients
To solve this, GMPO replaces the arithmetic mean with a geometric mean. Geometric means are way less sensitive to outliers, so this approach helps to improve stability. GMPO is shown to improve performance and helps avoid entropy collapse during RL training.
“GMPO is plug-and-play—simply replacing GRPO’s arithmetic mean with the geometric mean of token-level rewards, as the latter is inherently less sensitive to outliers.” - from GMPO paper
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G9oPQu1XcAAr6kP.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G9oPp0KWwAAPZxb.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
RL is computationally expensive, but researchers are quickly discovering speed ups. Olmo 3 does a great job of outlining the key tricks that helped to make RL more efficient:
1. A fully-asynchronous, off-policy RL setup is used that reduces idle time by allowing inference and model updates to continue running without waiting for all components to finish.
2. Continuous batching is used to constantly enqueue new inference requests in real-time as generations finish.
3. To compensate for examples removed by active sampling, OlmoRL—due to its asynchronous setup—can just continue sampling and filtering examples until the desired batch size is reached.
4. Inflight updates to the model weights being used for inference are performed without pausing generation or clearing the KV cache, which is found to improve throughput by ~4× with no deterioration in accuracy.
When applied in tandem, these tricks can cut RL training time in half without impacting performance.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
RL is notoriously unstable, and this gets worse when training MoEs because of expert volatility. Basically, if we run multiple consecutive policy updates over the same rollouts (as in GRPO), the experts that are selected tend to change a lot. This can lead to drastic fluctuation in importance ratios and, in turn, instability. It also gets worse for deeper MoEs.
"After one or more gradient updates, the experts activated for the same response can change significantly... with the 48-layer Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base model, after each RL gradient update and for the same rollout sample, there are roughly 10% of the experts activated under the new policy that are different from those under the old policy." - GSPO paper
Many papers have been published for making RL more stable with MoEs in particular. Interestingly though, we can actually drastically improve stability using a very simple approach called expert / routing replay. You just cache the experts that were used when a rollout was generated and use the same experts for all policy updates over this data.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G9y7vN8XAAAWPGA.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Vanilla GRPO has shortcomings that hinder RL training at scale. Here is a list of tricks and best practices for improving GRPO…
A full overview of these methods with paper references can be found in the corresponding blog post (see comments).
(1) Clip Higher: We decouple the upper and lower clipping bounds in GRPO, which restricts updates less on lower probability (exploration) tokens. This encourages exploration and helps to mitigate issues with entropy collapse during RL training.
(2) Dynamic Sampling: Throughout training, the ratio of problems solved perfectly by our policy increases. These problems—and problems with no valid solutions—have zero advantage and, therefore, zero contribution to the policy gradient. Dynamic sampling removes such examples from the batch, ensuring that all examples contribute meaningfully to the gradient.
(3) Token-level Loss: GRPO has a length bias that is introduced by averaging token-level losses in each sequence. Multiple papers have proposed solutions for this issue. For example, we can sum token-level losses over the sequence and divide by a fixed constant or average token-level losses over the entire batch instead of the sequence level.
(4) Alternative Aggregation: There are many other papers that adopt a better approach for aggregating token-level losses. For example, Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) computes all losses on the sequence level, while Geometric Mean Policy Optimization (GMPO) uses a geometric mean to improve robustness of the loss to outlier token-level losses.
(5) Overlong Rewards: We usually penalize rollouts that go beyond a maximum sequence length in RL, but this is not always optimal! For example, what if the policy has a great / valid reasoning trace that’s just too long? Instead, we can use a softer punishment strategy that dynamically increases the overlong penalty as the completion gets longer.
(6) No Standard Deviation: The GRPO advantage formulation divides normalized rewards by the standard deviation of rewards in the group, which causes the advantage to become very large for questions that are either too easy or too hard. We can solve this by just removing the division by standard deviation from the advantage formulation.
(7) Truncated Importance Sampling (TIS): Using separate engines for sampling rollouts and performing policy updates (e.g., vLLM + FSDP) can lead to a mismatch in log probabilities for completions. To correct for this mismatch, we can multiply the policy gradient by a (truncated) importance ratio between the probabilities produced by each engine.
(8) Clipped Importance Sampling Weight Policy Optimization (CISPO) introduces a soft clipping mechanism that ensures all tokens contribute to the policy gradient. The importance ratio is treated as a constant, but it is not backpropagated. This allows clipped tokens to have a capped contribution, rather than being eliminated from the policy gradient (as in GRPO).

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
RL is actually pretty good at continual learning (depending on how you define it). These results make me feel like RL-based continually learning is possible quite achievable...
Continual learning has recently become a popular topic of discussion. In order to maximize the utility of an LLM, this model needs to actively learn as it is used (i.e., on-the-job learning like humans). Currently, model utility is difficult to unlock because LLMs struggle to adapt or improve autonomously as they are used.
Setup. As a proxy for continual learning, consider a continual post-training setup with T datasets {D_1, D_2, ..., D_T}. Given a base model (e.g., an existing Instruct model), we can sequentially train over each of these datasets. This mimics continual learning behavior, where the LLM is exposed and trained on new tasks over time. This is (obviously) not a perfect proxy, but it's an informative empirical setup.
Metrics. To evaluate the model in terms of continual learning ability, we can consider two metrics:
1. Average accuracy of the model on test sets for all datasets after continual post-training completes.
2. Forgetting measure captures average difference between final accuracy of a task and the best accuracy achieved for that task throughout continual training.
When we compare multi-task SFT training, sequential SFT and sequential RL (GRPO / RLOO) over a set of downstream training datasets, we see that
(1) SFT leads to catastrophic forgetting of previously learned tasks during continual post-training on downstream tasks. Final average accuracy of 54% (much lower than multi-task learning with SFT, 62.9%).
(2) SFT degrades general capabilities too; e.g., 52.1% → 40.1% on MMMU.
(3) RL is naturally robust to forgetting. The forgetting measure is only -2.3%, and final average accuracy is 60%, which is close to upper bound of 62.9% achieved by multi-task SFT.
(4) RL maintains (and even improves) general model capabilities. For example, MMMU improves by 2.1% and POPE improves by 1.9% when running sequential GRPO-based RL training.
RL seems to be very good at maintaining and adding to model capabilities over time naturally! There are not even any replay buffers used for these results. As a disclaimer, there is still a ton of work left to figure out how continual learning would be defined in the real world, and it's possible this sim-to-real gap between proxy benchmarks like this and real life is huge.
“Without any data replay, continual post-training with RL can achieve comparable performance with that of multi-task training, which is not achievable even when equipping SFT with continual learning strategies.”
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G-FsUypXUAEkd57.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Another interesting note about RL being good at continual learning: the continual learning abilities of RL do not seem to come from KL divergence.
Most reasoning models use no KL divergence during RL training, but many RL training setups use a KL divergence penalty (either in the reward or the loss / objective) by default. Therefore, the ability of RL-based continual learning to not forget old information could be simply due to using this KL divergence.
When we test RL (GRPO) training with and without KL divergence in a continual learning setup (i.e., sequential training on several disjoint benchmarks), both achieve similar levels of performance. Performance is measured in terms of average accuracy across benchmarks and the amount of degradation in benchmark accuracy (i.e., delta between best and worst performance on a benchmark) throughout continual learning.
RL seems to be naturally prone to forgetting with and without the KL divergence term. Continual learning abilities are characteristic of RL, rather than an artifact of KL divergence.
Authors do note however that using KL divergence does improve stability of RL-based continual learning. Without KL divergence, they have to restart the continual learning pipeline several times for the model to converge. However, this might be an artifact of the RL training setup and exact GRPO settings (maybe can be fixed with DAPO-style tweaks).
Continual learning abilities also do not seem to be an artifact of using long CoT reasoning. Outputting a reasoning trace allows the model to enhance its performance in general, but it does not directly contribute to continual learning abilities (i.e., the model can avoid forgetting with our without a reasoning trace).
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G-J8dpxXEAAHBzk.jpg

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
Group Reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (GDPO) is a great extension of GRPO to multi-reward RL training setups...
Multi-reward. Sometimes, our reward in RL is not just a single number. We could have multiple sources of reward per prompt / completion! In other words:
full_reward = reward_1 + reward_2 + ...
A classic example of a multi-reward scenario is the standard training setup for reasoning models. Most reasoning models are trained with (i) verifiable reward and (ii) format reward that forces the model to output a reasoning trace with <think> </think> tokens.
How does GRPO handle this? In GRPO, we compute the advantage by normalizing over the full_reward. However, this approach collapses the reward signal, as sub-components of the reward are simply aggregated in a sum prior to normalization. This can lead to less distinct advantage groups and worse convergence.
Concrete example. Assume we have a prompt / completion that receives two rewards: r1 = +8 and r2 = +4. Assume the average full reward is 10, but the average r1 and r2 is 10 and 1, respectively. In this case, the advantage of the full reward is only slightly positive, but the advantage of r2 is actually quite large! Vanilla GRPO-style advantage estimates do not capture / reward the granular advantage of the r2 sub-reward.
The fix. To avoid this collapse of the reward signal, GDPO performs a separately GRPO-style normalization of each reward term separately as a first step prior to adding the rewards together. This is found to preserve distinct advantage groups and improve convergence / performance in multi-reward scenarios. Put simply, we view advantage individually for each sub-reward, rather than computing the advantage of the full-reward.
Impact. I think this is a really useful idea! To illustrate why this idea is useful, we should note that mixing reward signals seems to be a practical struggle even for the best reasoning models. Specifically, we often see that:
- Reasoning models are very good at producing correct output in a verifiable setting (i.e., the verifiable reward).
- Reasoning models may struggle with other attributes (e.g., formatting, instruction following, human-readability, etc.) more than traditional chat LLMs.
I believe these issues will gradually diminish with proposals such as GDPO. Over time, we will learn how to more effectively combine disparate reward signals and, as a result, train LLMs that find better multi-objective optima across many desirable characteristics.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
SFT / RL training objectives are equivalent to forward / reverse KL divergence. This is commonly cited in papers but hasn't always been trivial for me to understand, so I derived both cases below for reference...
Notation: Let's assume p* is out target distribution (for SFT this is the distribution over our training dataset, for RL this is the optimal policy we are trying to find via exploration) and p_t is our current policy.
SFT = Forward KL Objective
SFT uses a negative log-likelihood objective, or a cross-entropy loss over ground-truth next tokens. This is equivalent to the forward KL divergence, which we can prove as follows:
D_KL(p* || p_t) = E_{x ~ p*} [log(p*(x)) - log(p_t(x))]
= E_{x ~ p*} [log(p*(x))] - E_{x ~ p*} [log(p_t(x))]
= <entropy of target distribution> - <cross entropy>
In the above expression, the entropy of our target distribution is a constant, so minimizing forward KL is equivalent to minimizing negative log-likelihood.
RL = Reverse KL Objective
In RL, we are maximizing the reward of on-policy completions (i.e., sampled from our policy p_t), as well as minimizing kl divergence w.r.t. a reference policy:
\max_{p} E_{x ~ p} [reward(x)] - beta * D_KL(p || p_ref)
From this objective, we can derive a closed-form expression for the solution / optimal policy (also used to derive the DPO loss!):
p* = 1 / Z * p_ref(x) * exp( r(x) / beta)
where Z is the partition function. If we assume that this optimal policy is our target distribution, then we can show that maximizing the RL objective is equivalent to minimizing the reverse KL to this target distribution:
D_KL (p_t || p*) = E_{x ~ p_t} [log(p_t(x)) - log(p*(x))]
= E_{x ~ p_t} [log(p_t(x)) - log(p_ref(x)) + log(Z) - (r(x) / beta)
=- (1 / beta) E_{x ~ p_t} [r(x)] + D_KL(p_t || p_ref) + log(z)
As we can see, the final term above is the negative of our objective for RL (plus a scaling fractor of 1 / beta and an additional constant). Therefore, minimizing this objective (the reverse KL divergence) will maximize the standard RL objective!
What is the difference?
The key difference here between the forward and reverse KL is how we are sampling. SFT / forward KL samples from a dataset; x ~p*, where our dataset is p* because we are trying to minimize negative log-likelihood over the data). In contrast, RL / reverse KL is performing on-policy sampling; x ~ p_t, where p_t is our current policy.
This leads to some interesting mode-seeking versus mode-covering behavior that provides useful intuition for the mechanics of SFT and RL (will cover soon in a follow-up).

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
The SFT and RL training objectives can be interpreted in terms of KL divergence. Up to a constant, SFT minimizes forward KL divergence, while RL minimizes reverse KL divergence. This equivalence provides intuition for the unique mechanics of these learning algorithms.
Forward & Reverse KL Definition
The KL divergence is a measure for the divergence / difference between two probability distributions. For two probability distributions P and Q, we can define a forward and a reverse KL divergence as follows:
Forward: D_KL(P || Q) = E_{x ~ P} [log(P(x)) - log(Q(x))]
Reverse: D_KL(Q || P) = E_{x ~ Q} [log(Q(x)) − log(P(x))]
In the context of LLMs, our probability distributions are usually probability distributions over completions sampled from the LLM. A key difference between forward / reverse KL divergence lies in the sampling–the distribution from which we sample for the expectation changes. Depending on if we are using forward or reverse KL, we are either sampling from our dataset (offline) or sampling from the LLM itself (on-policy / online). We will directly see this concept used in the context of SFT and RL training below.
SFT ≈ forward KL
Let’s call our data distribution p*, and we can sample an example from our SFT dataset as x ~ p*. With this notation, the training objective for SFT is the negative log-likelihood:
E_{x ~ p*} [-log(p_t(x))]
Then, we can show the following for the relationship between this objective and the forward KL divergence:
D_KL(p* || p_t) = constant - E_{x ~ p*} [log(p_t(x))]
Where the right-hand-side here is our SFT objective, so SFT == forward KL divergence up to a constant. Minimizing both functions gives us the same result!
RL ≈ reverse KL
Let’s denote our current policy in RL as p_t and our reference policy as p_ref. We are trying to maximize the following objective:
E_{x ~ p_t} [reward(x)] - beta * D_KL(p_t || p_ref)
Where beta is the scaling factor for KL regularization. Note that this KL divergence is a regularization term in the RL objective and is unrelated to the relation we are exploring between KL and our training objectives.
From here, we can show the following:
D_KL (p_t || p*) = - (1 / beta) E_{x ~ p_t} [r(x)] + D_KL(p_t || p_ref) + constant
As we can see, this is the reverse KL divergence relative to the SFT expression. And, the quality here shows that this expression is equal to our RL objective (plus a constant and a scaling factor of 1 / beta).
Mode-Seeking versus Mode-Covering
What does this actually tell us about these training objectives?
SFT minimizes negative log-likelihood over a dataset, which is equivalent to minimizing the forward KL divergence. This is a mode-covering objective. Our model is heavily penalized for assigning low probability to any completion that is found in the data—the model must “spread” its probability mass across all possible completions or modes in the data.
On the other hand, RL maximizes the rewards of on-policy completions. This is equivalent to a reverse KL objective and is mode-seeking. The model emphasizes high-reward outputs, even at the cost of ignoring some output modes.
In SFT, the model’s loss increases exponentially if we assign near-zero probability to any completion in the dataset—this is due to the shape of the negative log-likelihood curve! Such a property is not true of RL, as we are simply maximizing the reward of on-policy completions. Assigning near-zero probability to a completion will prevent this particular completion from being sampled during RL, but reward can still be maximized over completions that are covered.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
summary:
TIL you can use a logistic / ranking loss formulation for knowledge distillation with LLMs. I'm most familiar with using either SFT / KL divergence objective, but using a logistic loss is pretty interesting!
How does it work? We look at the top-K logits from the teacher and create pairs between tokens k and l, where the teacher assigns a higher probability to k than l. Then, we look at the same pairs in the student and use a logistic / ranking objective that maximizes the margin between tokens k and l in the student. In other words, we train the student to rank the tokens in its next token prediction distribution similarly to the teacher.
This is a standard logistic loss. But, it's applied at the token level and pairs of chosen / rejected tokens are mined from the next token distribution of the teacher. This is a really neat / clever formulation for distillation. Great exercise for testing PyTorch knowledge (and maybe even a good interview question)!
